subtopic: RIGHT OF MEMBERS NOT TO DISCLOSE SOURCES OF INFORMATION-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prince Albert):
subtopic: RIGHT OF MEMBERS NOT TO DISCLOSE SOURCES OF INFORMATION-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity having to do with a judgment by the Ontario Court of Appeal on a motion as to whether a member of the legislature-and this applies, of course, to members of parliament-must disclose his confidential source of information.
The finding of the court was that information supplied to a member in confidence is not privileged from being revealed and, as the Globe and Mail points out in an historic landmark editorial in today's issue, the ending of protection against having to reveal confidential information given to members of parliament will pretty well put a stop to information being available. This is no criticism of the majority judgment of the court. That is the law now. But I ask leave, sir, to quote from the dissenting judgment of the Honourable Mr. Justice Weatherston. He said in part:
It has long been a major part of his (a member's) responsibilities to intercede on behalf of his constituents who claim to be oppressed by governmental bureaucracy and to bring to the notice of the government cases where legislation is thought to be working unfairly ... In all these cases the member may rely on information given to him in confidence. His effectiveness as a member may depend on confidences given and received, and the courts should respect those confidences unless the public interest clearly compels a breach of them.
This judgment, as I see it, will go a long way to emasculating parliament. Unless action is taken and legislation passed that members shall not be required to reveal their confidential sources of information, the lips of many Canadians will be sealed. All through the years I have personally taken the stand that under no circumstances would I reveal such information, and I think that is the general feeling of members of the House of Commons.
I would, therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski):
That this House assert the right of members to secure information confidentially and not be required, except in cases of treason or felony, to reveal the sources thereof.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN PRICE OF BEEF-ACTION TO HOLD DOWN FOOD PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council. According to reports of this past weekend, beef prices in Canada will increase by a full 18 cents a pound by the end of this week compared to the price per pound of last week. This increase will be the most dramatic in the history of Canadian beef prices.
Keeping in mind the AIB announcement last week that food prices rose a full 19 per cent last year, I ask the Deputy Prime Minister when the House can expect to hear from the government on the promise of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs last week that the government intended to do something about constantly escalating food prices in the country.

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN PRICE OF BEEF-ACTION TO HOLD DOWN FOOD PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like the hon. member, I read the weekend press which described the price paid for beef on Friday and the projected effect this price may have on retail levels. No one is certain, but I am not using that as a method of escaping from the prospect that beef prices indeed may increase.
As the hon. member knows, we have already taken steps to increase import quotas and to assist consumers who may be faced with rising prices. I have also read what the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs said last week in the House, that in respect of a number of situations he would like to check them out and report back to the hon. member. I will attempt to ensure that this is done.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN PRICE OF BEEF-ACTION TO HOLD DOWN FOOD PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, these are the same promises of future investigations from the Deputy Prime Minister that we have received for the past three weeks from the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. In the meantime, prices keep going up, not down.
Has the government considered the implications of the report a few weeks ago of the Economic Council, which showed profits per unit of output in the food and beverage industry had risen some 65 per cent in 18-month period ending in the third quarter of 1978, and that profits during the same period went up to the "highest level in the last 15 years"?
Given that this is the clearest possible evidence of excess profiteering, and given the fact that the head of the agency which made this report said that in view of these profit increases, firms should show restraint in the months ahead, will the Deputy Prime Minister tell us what, specifically, the government plans to do to ensure that price restraint is exercised so that consumers will see some levelling off in these increases?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN PRICE OF BEEF-ACTION TO HOLD DOWN FOOD PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it may be the hon. member, in referring to the increased level of beef prices, should bear in
February 5, 1979

mind that there is a delicate relationship between the supply of beef products and the consumer price. If he had read in more detail over the weekend, he would understand that one of the reasons prices are rising at the present time is because of a decrease in supply following a reluctance on the part of cattlemen in previous years, resulting from lower prices, to build up their herds.
The hon. member has to take a more balanced and broad view on price movements rather than just focusing on immediate consumer interests which are not the only interests involved in this situation. As I have said to the hon. member, we have taken some steps already during this current parliament to assist consumers in respect of increasing prices.
Having regard to the report to which the hon. member has referred, I regret to advise him that I have not read it, I do not have the statistics at my fingertips and I will not say that I have given consideration to the various statistical points he has made.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Deputy Prime Minister took a long time in giving an answer to the question I put to him in the first place. The question I should like him to deal with now is the broader one regarding food price increases.
The Economic Council of Canada has indicated that profits in that industry for the last 18 months, going into the third quarter of 1978, were up 91 per cent, and that price increases for the same period have gone up 65 per cent. The head of the institute that produced the study on behalf of the government indicated that measures should be taken now to keep prices down, because profits are very high.
I should like to ask the Deputy Prime Minister specifically in this area whether the government intends to bring forward particular measures which will respond to the requests that price increases be kept down in coming months because profits have already been excessively high in the past 18 months.

Minister of Transport said that the government is in negotiation with this group. In fact, no negotiations are going on.

subtopic: CANADA'S ABILITY TO COPE WITH PETROLEUM SHORTAGE IN EVENT IRAN REDUCES OIL PRODUCTION
CANADA'S ABILITY TO COPE WITH PETROLEUM SHORTAGE IN EVENT IRAN REDUCES OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I put a question to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources with respect to the continuing crisis in Iran, and particularly the question of petroleum supplies from that country.
The United States is now actively considering the prospect of rationing petroleum products. Just this weekend, certain Iranian spokesmen were suggesting a permanent cutback of 40 per cent in production. Is Canada prepared to cope with a possible North American shortage of petroleum, either in co-operation with the United States or otherwise, and to what countries may we look for new sources of supply should that become necessary?

speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: CANADA'S ABILITY TO COPE WITH PETROLEUM SHORTAGE IN EVENT IRAN REDUCES OIL PRODUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the situation is serious. It is by no means a panic situation at the present time, but it is serious. We may well be facing reductions in supply in the coming months.
At the present time, the situation is still manageable. We are making every effort to ensure that there will be supplies for Canadian refineries in eastern Canada. We are looking to other sources of supply, particularly Mexico, to replace the Iranian production, and to Venezuela. Venezuela, of course, is under pressure from other countries. Venezuela has been our major supplier, supplying some 40 per cent of our imports. I

February 5, 1979

have received personal assurances from Venezuela that those supplies will continue to Canada. We are also working in Venezuela, trying to work out new opportunities with regard to heavy oils. That program is well under way between Petro-Canada and Petroleos de Venezuela.
As far as Mexico is concerned, again Petro-Canada will be the major player on behalf of Canada, working with the Mexican national oil company which handles all exports of oil from Mexico-Pemex. I believe these measures will help to assure Canadians of a continuing source of supply and reduce our dependence on Middle Eastern crude.

speakeroldname: Mr. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
subsubtopic: USE OF EMERGENCY LOCATOR TRANSMITTERS IN AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. In December, 1977, a jet crashed at Churchill Falls, resulting in the loss of eight people, two of whom died of exposure because the aircraft was not discovered for 48 hours, despite the fact it was only a mile from the runway. There was no emergency locator transmitter aboard, because DOT had ordered them removed.
Can the minister advise whether the Deprtment of Transport has ordered all Canadian and civil aircraft to again start using emergency locator transmitters, or what is the situation in that regard?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: USE OF EMERGENCY LOCATOR TRANSMITTERS IN AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the situation is now one of some ability on the part of aircraft to use transmitters, particularly if they are of the type that is safe.
The hon. member knows the reason for discontinuing their use. It was the discovery that the lithium batteries in the transmitters were, in fact, themselves a source of danger and could have been the cause of accidents. In order to avoid that happening, they were removed. Work has been done on finding batteries that are satisfactory. There has been some progress, although not yet enough to ensure that there will be an ELT on every aircraft.

subsubtopic: USE OF EMERGENCY LOCATOR TRANSMITTERS IN AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
As the minister probably knows, there has been a magisterial inquiry under way in Newfoundland into the deaths from that crash. Captain Powick of the Search and Rescue centre at Halifax stated at that time that he knows of no dangerous incident involving military aircraft, and that it is costing the taxpayer millions of dollars to search for aircraft that do not have ELTs on board. He said he could see no reason not to have ELTs aboard aircraft, that sufficient time has elapsed to find a suitable replacement for the lithium battery.
What is the minister's department doing? A year has gone by, and anybody who travels on an aircraft today has his life in jeopardy, if he survives a crash, because there are no ELTs on these aircraft. When will the minister show a sense of urgency about the installation of ELTs? They have them in the United States without lithium batteries. When does the minister propose to act?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: USE OF EMERGENCY LOCATOR TRANSMITTERS IN AIRCRAFT
speechtext:
The hon. member says they have them in the United States without lithium batteries. The problem in Canada which made special batteries necessary is the extremely cold weather which is much more common in this part of the world than it is farther south. Perhaps the hon. member does not know that. In Canada, these batteries must be able to work under a variety of conditions, including temperatures well below zero. It is this which led to the search for new batteries to replace the lithium batteries. Obviously, technological development can be forced only so far, but some batteries of an improved kind are now being made and some are available. However, we are not yet at a point at which we can require that every aircraft instals them.
The hon. member told us someone had said he knew of no incidents. Well, our department does know of some incidents and they have been quoted in answers given in this House: lithium-powered batteries have actually exploded in aircraft, becoming such a clear danger that they had to be removed. No amount of protestation on the part of the hon. member will alter that fact.
February 5, 1979

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subsubtopic: MR. MCGRATH-REPLY OF DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order having to do with a question I put to the Deputy Prime Minister today following a question which had been raised by the Leader of the New Democratic Party. It had to do with the question of profiteering. The Deputy Prime Minister took the opportunity to twist my question around; uncharacteristically he imputed motives to me by accusing me of saying I was accusing the beef producers of profiteering.
The whole thrust of my question had to do with the sharp increase of stockyard prices for beef last week and the report in the weekend press by two of the leading supermarkets that beef prices would rise by 10 cents a pound as of Monday. We are told it takes anywhere from two to three weeks for beef prices to work their way through the system, as was the case last June when beef prices went down; it took three weeks for the decrease to reach consumers. My question was: What steps is the government taking to ensure that no profiteering is
Point of Order-Mr. Mazankowski
taking place at the expense of either producers or consumers? We have set up a centre for the study of productivity. I had hoped the Deputy Prime Minister would refer my question to that body. The acting minister, who appeared to be in a state of shock when I directed my question-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. MCGRATH-REPLY OF DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext: Order. The hon. member is aware, I am sure, that he has been airing a grievance about the answer given to his question and the treatment his question received during the question period. He has not come close to establishing any disorder; he has not advanced any procedural argument. If he has a point of order he has yet to persuade me that this is the case. Otherwise, I would be bound to permit everybody who did not like the answers they got during the question period to make similar use of this time.

subsubtopic: MR. MCGRATH-REPLY OF DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext:
I believe I do have a point of order, Mr. Speaker, and I raise it with great respect. You, sir, in your conduct of the question period, impose severe restrictions on hon. members asking questions, and rightly so. My point is that the same restrictions should be imposed on ministers when they reply. Otherwise, what happens? We had the example today of the Deputy Prime Minister making a cheap shot, knowing full well that somebody else would be recognized.
I did not state or impute in any way that profiteering was going on by beef producers. I was asking the minister to assure us that the government was taking steps to make certain that there was no profiteering taking place in the marketplace as a result of what happened last week to stockyard prices for beef. Surely there is a question of disorder involved here because the Deputy Prime Minister imputed motives to my question though there was no such suggestion in the question I asked. If Your Honour would take the time to examine the record I believe you would find that my point of order is valid.

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and President of Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. MCGRATH-REPLY OF DEPUTY PRIME MINISTER DURING QUESTION PERIOD

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order in regard to the great number of questions which have been on the order paper for a lengthy period of time not only in this session but also in other sessions. This is the only recourse a member of this House has to draw questions to the attention of the House, and I hope that the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) or his parliamentary secretary will take action in this regard.
I would like today to draw attention to four specific questions which are on the order paper in my name. I refer first to one which was placed there two years and eight months ago. It is a very simple question. It asks simply how many members of the Canadian Transport Commission and their wives have Air Canada passes. I do not see why it should take two years and eight months to compile an answer to such a simple question. The question to which I refer is question No. 4.
Question No. 5 concerns the office of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). Three years ago I asked for a breakdown of the $86,703 of public funds which had been spent on the office

February 5, 1979
Point of Order-Mr. Cossitt
of the Prime Minister. I raised this matter on a point of order one year ago. At that time two years had gone by and the question was not answered. The Prime Minister replied to this effect: "Let it be made public; put it in all the papers, I don't mind". After three years the answer is still not forthcoming.
The third question to which I would like to refer is question No. 9 dealing with the fingerprinting of public servants. The question asks how many have been fingerprinted. I know that the number would be very large. The question also asks why this invasion of privacy is taking place with regard even to those who are not engaged in jobs of a security nature. In such jobs such a procedure might be understandable, but that question has been on the order paper for two years, and it remains unanswered.
Finally, question No. 10 has been on the order paper one year and seven months. It deals with Martin Goldfarb and Goldfard Consultants of Toronto. The question deals with what contacts they have had with the government or with any government department regarding government business. I am not asking about the hundreds of thousands or millions of dollars they may have received from the Liberal party, just from the government. That question has been unanswered for one year and seven months.
There are other questions, and I think I have the right as a member of this House to rise each day I am here and draw attention to two or three questions which have not been answered. Today I have drawn attention to four.
The parliamentary secretary might rise in the tradition of his predecessors and point to the great percentages and tremendous work which has been done in answering questions, but I do not care whether 87 per cent, 88 per cent, 89 per cent or 90 per cent of questions have been answered. If hon. members opposite are avoiding questions which would embarrass the government on the eve of an election, I think it is high time the people of Canada realized the sham which is being perpetrated by this government.
Will the parliamentary secretary rise now and tell me when these four specific questions will be answered? After three years I think I have a right to know.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the debate adjourned on Friday I was dealing with the impact which the cutback in the health resources fund would have on the Rehabilitation International Congress which is scheduled to be held in Winnipeg during June of 1980. I complimented the minister for her attempts to deal with a very difficult situation in the face of the cutbacks which suddenly appeared following the television address of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on August 1.
The minister actually has a double problem because she is carrying the torch for promises which were made by her predecessor, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lalonde), who for a period of some five or six years when he had the responsibilities of minister of national health and welfare raised the level of expectation to unprecedented heights. Let me quote from a speech the hon. gentleman made on May 30 of 1973 in which he said that under the new social services legislation rehabilitation was to be given top priority to promote the principle of self-reliance among the handicapped. He said that governments and voluntary groups for too long had introduced programs which promoted dependence rather than independence. The minister stated, and I quote:
The handicapped have the right to be as independent as possible, the right to live like everyone in the community and the services they need to bring this about should be provided.
This refers to a question which the hon. member for Rose-dale was asking just a moment ago with respect to the cutback in home care services for the disabled. Then later on in his speech the former health minister spoke about a conference which was held by the disabled themselves.lt was one of the first conferences at which the disabled were provided the opportunity to speak for themselves and to express their wishes. The conference was funded by the federal government
February 5, 1979

and sponsored by the Canadian Rehabilitation Council for the Disabled. Here is the message that came out of this conference:
In every area the message was clear: They "wanted in": into employment, into community living, into maximum participation in community life, into the planning of systems and services designed to help them. At the same time they "wanted out": out of institutions, out of dead-end sheltered workshops, out of welfare, out of being pitied, out of being thrust on to the sidelines with a pension and a shrug.
This is a quotation from a speech which was delivered by the former minister of national health and welfare back in 1973.
One of the main problems with which the minister is wrestling as she faces a cutback in this important area is the necessity of providing adequate personnel resources. In a document which was tabled as Appendix "B" last November 27, at page 1555 of Hansard, we have some very revealing facts with respect to the inability of Canada to provide trained personnel resources to deal with the growing problems of rehabilitating the physically and mentally handicapped, and this is one of the most expensive areas of concern in the whole health and welfare fields.
Looking at the document which was tabled by the minister and printed as an appendix to Hansard, we find that it states that the number of biomedical engineers who had graduated in 1966 was 14; in 1976, some ten years later, that number had only increased to 39. The demand, of course, is far beyond that number. But what is even more revealing is the fact that occupational therapists who play a large role in the rehabilitation process numbered 78 in 1966, and in 1976 there were only 237 of them. I compare this with 3,800 nursing assistants in 1966 and 5,500 nursing assistants in 1976. You can see that the level is quite low by comparison, Mr. Speaker.
Physiotherapists, who are right on the Firing line in rehabilitation, numbered 232 in 1966 and 446 in 1976, as compared to 880 physicians in 1966 and 1,700 in 1976. So the time of fully trained medical doctors has been taken up in areas which could be delegated to paramedics such as physiotherapists.
There are no figures available for the training of doctors in physical medicine or physiatrists, so I presume they are not being trained anywhere in Canada, and of course an ordinary MD has great difficulty in coping with the particular demands of rehabilitation.
I had an interesting exchange of correspondence recently in company with the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) regarding the case of a young chap who is not a Canadian and had come from another country. He was taking his doctorate at the Chedoke Rehabilitation Centre at McMaster university in a very highly specialized field in the rehabilitation movement. He was being trained in the field of biomedical engineering with a special focus on studying human locomotor function and applying external electrical stimuli to activate paralysed muscles. This work is quite unique in Canada, in the world as a matter of fact, and actually this particular specialist is one of his kind in the world. So hon. members will see that we have a long way to go
Health Resources Fund Act
in training personnel in the rehabilitation field. It became necessary to approach the Department of Employment and Immigration, and this gentleman will be allowed to stay in Canada following his graduation and to serve in this way. But he is only one and we need hundreds of similarly trained personnel. Of course, there will be a setback in this area as a result of the cutback in the resource funding.
Another thought I have in this area is that the whole Field of geriatrics will be affected, the special care that is required for our senior citizens. They are a rapidly increasing percentage of the population; 15 per cent of Canadians will be in the geriatric age group by the end of the present century, and obviously with the slow progress we are making, we will not be prepared to meet the special health and welfare requirements of a senior citizen population. They are affected by all sorts of crippling diseases and disabling afflictions, and when you do not have personnel specially trained to deal with these problems, they constitute a crippling demand on health and welfare resources.
This is where one of our problems lies-the escalating cost of providing these services and meeting these needs at present. Insitutional care is not the answer, but this has been the answer we have unconsciously given in meeting this problem. Some of these institutions are referred to as human warehouses. What we want are the facilities, the home care, meals on wheels and attention in the home that will make it possible for the disabled person, the handicapped person and the older citizen to have the beneFit and the warmth of a home environment rather than eke out an existence in these cold human warehouses. We want to be able to add life to the years of Canada's disabled.
Let me conclude my remarks by saying that the whole emphasis of the Rehabilitation International Congress in Winnipeg in June, 1980 will be precisely on the points I have raised. The theme of the congress will be prevention and integration, the priorities for the 1980s. These are the areas where Canada is falling down because of the misplacement of our financial priorities. We could prevent a lot of crippling and disabling diseases if only we aimed our emphasis, our priorities, in the right direction.
There will be six preliminary seminars at the congress which will deal with major areas of concern. The seminar on special education will take place in Vancouver. The medical seminar will be in Kingston, the social needs seminar in Winnipeg and the organizational need seminar will also be in Winnipeg. In Toronto there will be a technical aid seminar which will be joined by the inter-agency from the United States and will bring together some 1,500 people to deal with the biomedical aspects of the rehabilitation movement. Toronto will also have a seminar on the vocational needs of Canada's disabled population.
Canada was fortunate to get the congress. I was privileged to be with the invitation committee which travelled to Tel Aviv in Israel in June of 1976 where we attended the Rehabilitation International Congress. There was pretty stiff competition, but the reason Canada was awarded the 1980 congress was that

February 5, 1979
Health Resources Fund Act
we could guarantee there would be a great breakthrough in social services for the handicapped.
I read some of the speeches of the hon. member for Out-remont concerning all the wonders which were just around the corner. As a result of that presentation Canada was selected, but unfortunately all we have at present is great hope and expectations. We can get it all together. As I said the other day, the minister has written to me indicating the problem in this regard and her support for the motion which I put before the House namely that we constitute a special subcommittee of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs to gather pertinent information from the voluntary organizations and have a report ready for the congress in 1980.
In December, 1977 I was privileged to go to New York and speak on behalf of Canada in support of the motion declaring 1981 as rehabilitation year. That motion was accepted unanimously, so that rehabilitation international year will flow out of the 1980 congress in Canada. The role of Canada is very large in all these areas, and of course the reputation of Canada is at stake. We must have something very concrete, not only in terms of hope and expectation, but also in terms of legislative proposals. Britain is ahead of us. It has had special legislation since 1971, and now has a minister of state for rehabilitation. We have a long way to go even to match that kind of progress.
I recognize the problems which the minister has as she struggles valiantly to meet the problems created by the sudden reversal of the Prime Minister in funding respecting health and welfare measures, and I should like to make some specific proposals. I hope we will get the subcommittee together as soon as possible in order to gather public sentiment and opinion in preparation for the time when it will be possible to proceed with the legislation. I trust the minister will be able to reconstitute the rehabilitation unit which existed at one time in the Department of National Health and Welfare. It was disbanded because we were moving toward the dawn of the new age respecting rehabilitation matters, as was promised by the hon. member for Outremont in his speeches a few years ago. We were to do away with some of the existing legislation and co-ordinate it under the new social services act.
There are excellent personnel in the Department of National Health and Welfare. I have met them at various conferences. They are competent in the field of rehabilitation. In a letter written on December 5, the minister indicated that it was her intention to reconstitute the rehabilitation unit. I hope people such as Andre LeBlanc, who has had broad experience in this field and has left it temporarily because of the disintegration of the rehabilitation unit within the department, will be called back into service, particularly in preparation for the 1980 congress to be held in Winnipeg. Also I trust it will be possible to have an advisory committee composed of representatives from the privte sector who are providing leadership in this field at the moment. They are ahead of the government in meeting the various needs. I hope an advisory committee will come out of the committee investigating the state of rehabilitation arts
in Canada as it moves across the country to hear representations from these people. It could advise the government on how to cut down the huge expenses and waste involved in meeting the needs of our handicapped population because of the lack of co-ordinated policies.
I hope the government will provide a resource centre upon which professionals in the field can call to obtain databank information on all available technical aids. The information centre could co-ordinate all activities and avoid costly duplication to taxpayers as various groups attempt to meet the very difficult problems of rehabilitation. I hope the health resources fund will be built up to such an extent that it will be possible to provide personnel. As I indicated a moment ago, the personnel training program is totally inadequate to provide the needed expertise. We require a sense of direction, rather than an ad hoc approach to fundamental health and welfare programs which are on again and off again, stop and start. Such programs only confuse and add to the waste in meeting needs.
We require a stable long-term program which will last at least three to five years. This is why I say the present program is quite inadequate. It is not good enough for the government to keep changing direction, to raise the hopes and expectations of the people who have held out for the past seven years awaiting a new social services legislation which would meet their needs adequately. This has not been done and this is why we criticize the program at the present time.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the contributions over the last few days respecting the legislation before the House. I believe this particular matter is one of the most important to occupy our attention. When we consider all the assets of life, health is one of the most important.
I should like to deal with the proposal of the government to eliminate the health resources fund. This has caused a great deal of dismay, not only in the Canadian medical community but in the respective provinces and among the public at large.
As this debate continues, there is a tendency to forget the details and the background information on the Health Resources Fund Act. The Health Resources Fund Act was established under the Pearson administration and given Royal Assent on July 11, 1966. At that time the government perceived a need for funding certain types of research in the medical field, teaching, medical and laboratory equipment, and research facilities in Canadian universities and hospitals. The fund was set up and $500 million was allocated and disbursed over a 15-year period as follows: $300 million to the provinces on a per capita basis; $25 million to the Atlantic provinces for joint projects; $175 million to be allocated by the governor in council for particular projects. Approximately $400 million has been spent. About one-fifth of the fund went to medical schools and major purpose buildings in the health science complex. Another one-fifth went to university hospitals. Some money went to affiliated hospitals. Approximately $23 million was contributed to dental schools with $76 million to nursing schools, auxiliary schools and other health and manpower training centres.

February 5, 1979_____________________________COMMONS
To my mind and to the minds of a great many Canadians, this fund was worth while and the money was well spent. By cancelling the health resources fund the government has stated it will save $84 million over a period of 2 years. The minister agreed both at the second reading stage of this bill and at third reading that the fund had been worth while and had done a lot of good for the people of Canada. After devoting a major part of her speech on second reading to saying how great the fund was, she then announced it was to be cancelled. The logic of this leaves one baffled. This was pointed out by my colleague, the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk), at second reading stage when he stated that either the fund is good and deserves support or it is bad and deserves to be cancelled. We find a paradox in that the minister says it is good but it is to be cancelled.
I think one of the reasons that she has taken this position was set out in her speech a few days ago when she said the objectives of the program had been completed. In the course of the debate several of my colleagues have pointed out activities in various areas which have either been left unfinished or untouched in this Field of endeavour involving the delivery of health care.
As we listened to other speakers we came to the conclusion that possibly the minister was speaking without a full understanding of the facts or in some way had missed the point of some of the legislative programs. Without question there are areas which have been left untouched, and there are groups of people, segments of our population, that have not been the recipients of adequate health delivery care. For these reasons we feel it is highly inappropriate at this time that this particular program should be eliminated. I would suggest that of all the places to cut expenditures, this type of program should be one of the last.
During the debates throughout the past months we on this side of the House have advised the government that if it is really interested in making some meaningful cuts in expenditures and trimming the expensive fat from its operations, it should pay more attention to the recommendations, observations and comments made in the Auditor General's report. Unfortunately, instead of doing that the government is moving in other directions, eliminating or reducing programs which have a direct bearing upon the personal needs and lives of individuals. This is very unfortunate because in doing so the government is leaving certain people and groups without the essential services necessary if they are to maintain adequate health and serve our country in a productive fashion.
As we consider this particular measure today it is reasonable, and certainly understandable, that we should take so much time in calling attention to the injustices of this cancellation, pointing out ways in which other expenditures can be cut without bringing to an end programs which have been of such importance to the people and the country.
One well-known expert in the area of medical research, for instance, has made a study that clearly shows that, for every dollar invested in research today, $20 will be saved in
DEBATES	____________2883
Health Resources Fund Act
ten years' time through dramatically reduced health costs. The cutting of research projects in any field does not necessarily save money, but it does in many cases increase the cost to the taxpayer or the individual citizen in Canada.
My colleague the hon. member for Athabasca cited a number of examples of this fact when speaking during another stage of the debate. Let me just refer to one of his statements. He said that it cost $41 million to develop the polio vaccine. That was the total cost. Since polio vaccine has been in use in Canada, beginning in 1955, Canada has saved $200 million per year in medical and health care costs. This is just one piece of successful research that has saved this country more than four times the total expenditure for research in each year since 1955. How can this government in the name of restraint downgrade medical research in such a way?
Some of my colleagues have referred to areas where medical research has not been provided the people of Canada. Reference has been made to the action of the minister and the government in respect of medical care for native people. I noticed that in one instance it was reduced, the next time it was increased, and then it was reduced again. It seems illogical that in an important area, such as this there should be an on-again, off-again, here-again, gone-again, "Flannigan" attitude toward medical care for our native people.
Just yesterday I picked up a publication called "Circlet" put out by the Union of National Defence Employees. The main article on the front page under the heading "Keep health units, Power says", states in part:
The Union of National Defence Employees is in the forefront of efforts to fight a reduction of health services to federal public employees across the country.
As part of Ottawa's announced restraint program, the Department of National Health and Welfare has announced it is closing a number of health units and is cutting back on the number of man-years for some others. At some Department of National Defence bases, nurses will be available for only part of each week.
The health and welfare department says that each department will be expected to take up the slack by improving available first-aid services.
Then the article refers to a statement of Mr. Joe Power, national president. It states:
Joe Power, UNDE national president, has taken the matter directly to Health Minister Monique Begin.
In a letter to the minister Dec. 22, Power protested "in the strongest terms possible" her department's decision to make an almost 25 per cent reduction in man-years for the public service occupational health program.
This next part is very significant I believe. It states:
The reduced health services are a false economy, the letter says. It points out that 27,900 work injuries in the federal public service between April 1, 1977 and March 31, 1978 resulted in a cost of more than $16.6 million.
It is impossible to estimate how much more time and money would be lost if injured workers were not to receive immediate fully-qualified medical attention, the UNDE president writes. However, the figure would probably be in the millions of dollars and thousands of hours, not to mention the possibilty of increased deaths.
I believe that it is false economy, when one is considering the health of the people of Canada, to introduce and to put

February 5, 1979
Health Resources Fund Act
into place restraints or cutbacks in this particular area. Surely there are other fields in which restraint could be exercised- and we have pointed these out-without removing programs that are of such a direct and urgent benefit to the people.
With regard to the allegation or charge that there have not been adequate discussions with the provinces, I would like to express my support for those contentions. It was rather surprising, after all the discussions with regard to negotiation and consultation with the provinces and with regard to how thoroughly various programs have been dealt with and carried out, to hear the minister say in her speech, as recorded at page 2810 of Hansard, dated February 1:
If I go back to the exact nature of this bill, which is to cancel the health resources fund a few years ahead of its natural termination date, I must acknowledge that many members complained in the committee about the fact that no consultation had taken place with the provinces on introducing an earlier cut-off date after which no new projects are to be approved. The fact is that there was very little time for specific consultation when the final decision was taken.
Those comments are rather significant in view of the fact that the government has reached the point where it would cut off a program worked out in consultation with the provinces, and on top of that say there was not sufficient time to consult with them to reduce the time frame of the program by approximately two years.
We tend to think of all these changes in terms of a reduction in the delivery of health services, its effect upon research and so on. I have in my hand a newsletter published by Canadians for Health Research which contains an editorial that I think is very pertinent to this question. It says:
Much has been said during the past two years about the effect of funding cutbacks on the Canadian scientific community and health care delivery system. What has not been stressed is that Canada has an obligation to the people of the world-
The obligations we have to our own people are fundamental, but here this newsletter is saying that Canada has an obligation to the people of the world.
-to provide knowledge and techniques to enable them to achieve minimal levels of health.
Officials of the World Health Organization speaking at the CHR National Conference pointed out that hundreds of millions of people suffer from severe tropical diseases-
And it goes on to mention some diseases, the names of which I cannot pronounce.
-for which there are no cures. The development of new technologies is essential if advances in the control of these major parasitic diseases are to be achieved. The third world does not have the academic and technical resources to do the research on these diseases. Canada does. We therefore have a moral responsibility to provide not only massive amounts of foreign aid to purchase advanced technological products, but to export our knowledge in the field of biomedical research.
Those comments illustrate very clearly that by making a cut such as the government is proposing in this bill, it is affecting not only the health care services within Canada but also those services which could be and should be provided to other parts of the world.
We hear a great deal about consultation between the provinces and the federal government today. It seems to me that

the government ought to take another look at this whole area and reassess their attitude toward provincial responsibility and participation in these programs. At the time the medical care bill was introduced there was a great deal of discussion, and at one point it was thought that the bill would flounder and not be passed, because some of the provinces were not willing to enter into the program as proposed. But finally, after a great deal of arm-twisting, the provinces came in and the medicare plan was put into operation. In this instance the federal government applied strong-tongue tactics-I was about to say strong-arm tactics, but that is not quite right-in order to get the provinces to accept medicare, but just a short while ago the government brought in a measure which put a cap on the expenditures, and the result was that the provincial governments were saddled with additional expenses as far as that particular program was concerned.
Once again, after making a commitment and working out this program with the provinces, the government is reneging and leaving the provinces holding the bag. This is very unfair to the provinces. The result is that there is a great deal of resentment that would not be there had the government taken a more positive position and attitude in their deliberations and discussions with the provinces. This is why we say that the damage to our confederation has been done by a government which fails to recognize the provinces as partners in confederation. I have said before that the relationship between the two levels of government has deteriorated to the point where there is suspicion and distrust, which should not be.
As a result of this bill, the provinces will once again have to accept the fact that another program has been curtailed and, in this case, eliminated two years prior to its cut-off date. The protests have come from this side of the House, and I add my voice to those who have already spoken. But regardless of the protests and representations made, the government will maintain this attitude, which will continue to prevail until the time comes when it is replaced by a government which is more sensitive to the needs of Canadians, a government with policies which are designed to meet those needs in a constructive and adequate fashion.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill before us, as hon. members know, is to eliminate the health resources fund and, in effect, the allocation of $80 million that still remains in the fund which, under normal circumstances, would be paid out to the provinces for essential medical-diagnostic facilities. I, too, would like to add my words of opposition to the elimination of this fund.
I believe that there are many things we can do as a country to improve the health and well-being of Canadian citizens. I want to spend a few minutes on an area which I think is overlooked by almost all modern industrial societies, Mr. Speaker. It is an area, quite frankly, in which all political parties when they are in office have created disaster, and that is nutrition and preventive medicine. I think this is one of the real issues, challenges, perhaps one of the results of an industrial society that the world is overlooking, and I want to make some non-partisan remarks about it.
February 5, 1979

I recall speaking to a senior official in the Saskatchewan government a couple of years ago and asking him what was new in the area of health. He replied, "We have done everything we have to do. We have medicare, hospitalization, cancer programs, eye glasses programs, drug prescription programs and the like." I said, "I commend you. The government of Saskatchewan has led the way in health care in this country and in North America, but in my opinion it has just begun."
Let us look at some of the things I am speaking about, Mr. Speaker, as they relate to the whole area of health in the industrialized world, particularly in the areas of nutrition and preventive medicine. In the United States Senator George McGovern and a team completed a comprehensive study of health in that country about two years ago. They linked six of the leading causes of death to diet and the types of food people eat. They said that North Americans eat far too much sugar, fats and salty foods-that we are digging our graves with our teeth, as the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) has just commented. The World Health Organization has said that about 90 per cent of cancers are caused by the environment and that a large part of that environment is the type of food we consume.
In a white paper produced about three years ago the Food Prices Review Board said that in 1972 about 40 per cent of the hospital days in this country were as a result of the malnutrition of the Canadian people, and the cost was around $2 billion. The former head of Nutrition Canada, a renowned scientist named Dr. Zak Sabry, about the same time said it probably cost more than $2 billion per year. He said that on an annual basis the total cost of poor nutrition to Canada is about $7 billion to $8 billion, of which about $2.5 billion could be saved each year through improved nutrition.
Heart disease was virtually unknown prior to the turn of the century. Many studies link the type of food we eat with the type of ailment. Another interesting report is one which was issued by the Quebec government. Governments of all political stripes in this country have not placed a high enough priority on preventive medicine and nutrition. Last year the federal government, the provinces and municipalities spent on nutrition and nutritional education only about 1 per cent of what the food retailing and processing industries spent on promoting food. Breakfast cereals that are 50 or 60 per cent sugar and things like that which are detrimental to health were promoted.
The Quebec government issued a paper entitled "Une Politique Quebecoise en Matiere de Nutrition" which is a comprehensive study of the nutritional problems of people in this country. They are implementing some of the proposals and I hope this will act as a vanguard in this field, as did the actions of the Saskatchewan government in years gone by in the field on the delivery of health services to everyone regardless of income. The document reports on the state of nutrition in this country. Many people claim that Canadians are not malnourished while other people say we suffer from a great deal of malnutrition.
Health Resources Fund Act
The report also points out that the consumption of alcohol in this country has increased drastically in the last few years. In this regard it states:

It has recently been demonstrated that between 10 and 20 per cent of total calories consumed by the North American adult come under the form of alcool.
And, further:
Mortality due to liver cirrhosis has registered a gross increase of nearly 200 per cent during the last twenty years. The number of deaths has increased from 195 cases in 1951 to 558 in 1971.

So as we see, Mr. Speaker, the types of food and beverages we consumer today lead to very serious health problems and in many cases lead to deaths which should not occur.
A study carried out a few years ago by Nutrition Canada found that one and one-half million Canadians suffered from malnutrition of one form or another. That means they lack the vitamins and minerals that are necessary for the body to function properly.
Some of the information in that report is startling. For example, in this country about 70 per cent of old age pensioners suffer from calcium deficiency. Imagine that in a country with the capacity to produce an unlimited volume of milk, where two years ago farmers were throwing milk away on the steps of the House of Commons because they did not receive a decent price for it in the market, if they could find a market. The report also found that 44 per cent of Canadians had iron deficiency and 60 per cent had vitamin D deficiency. And the list goes on, Mr. Speaker.
The same thing is true in the United States. According to studies in that country in 1955, about 60 per cent of the population had a well-balanced diet. In 1965, ten years later, about 50 per cent of the population had a well-balanced diet.
If we study our eating patterns since World War II, we will find them absolutely frightening for the future of health in this industrialized society. The consumption of dairy products has dropped by 23 per cent, the consumption of fresh fruit by 25 per cent, while the consumption of soft drinks has increased by 80 per cent. In some cases children in the United States average three soft drinks per day. The consumption of pastries has increased by 80 per cent, and of potato chips by 85 per cent. Is it any wonder that the medical experts tell us today that nearly half the adult Canadian population is overweight? And I am not looking at the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles)! I do not intend to name names. However, about one half of the Canadian population is obese. That problem can be traced back to the type of diet we have. I was talking about some changes in eating patterns in the United States. The same is true in this country.
One need only look to the Nutrition Canada surveys to find that what is occurring in the United States is also occurring in Canada. I have a study here. The years 1905 to 1910 are given a basic index of 100. You can trace the consumption of certain

February 5, 1979
Health Resources Fund Act
products, one of them being refined sugar. In the years 19051910, the base was 100. In 1973 the base index went up to about 140 or 145. Meat went up to between 145 and 150. If you look at dairy products or cereals and flour, that went down to about 55 or 60, reflecting similar eating patterns that one sees in the United States. The bill before us will eliminate the health resources fund. That $80 million could be spent very usefully on trying to come up with programs and policies which will show Canadians the need to become concerned with the types of food they are eating and with the food system we have in this country.
Many people say that we live longer today, that people do not die as young as they used to. I suggest we take a good look at that argument. If we look at the arguments, facts and data, one point comes very clearly to mind as to why the lifespan is longer now than in 1900. Because of modern medicines and hospitals, we have been able to combat the problem of infant mortality. Babies are not dying as a result of diseases they died of some 70 or 80 years ago. In addition, we have penicillin which has reduced the death rate of people of all ages. If you compare the life expectancy of people over 21 in the year 1900 with the years 1978 and 1979, you find that life expectancy has not gone up significantly. But despite modern medicine, hospitals, surgery, medicare and other services, the average lifespan in Canada in the past 70 or 80 years has not to any significant degree lengthened. The main part of the reason is our food system.
Let us look briefly at the food we consume. The foods we consume in this country contain about 1,800 chemicals or artificial additives. We eat more processed or heavily manufactured foods than ever before. Many people say, "So what?" I remind them that the more food is manufactured or processed, the more vital minerals and vitamins are refined out of that food. I will use the example of canned peas which many of us pick up on the supermarket shelves. When you open a can of peas, warm them on the stove and then consume them, 94 per cent of the food value will have been lost. Only about 6 per cent of the food value remains compared to the value you would get from peas picked fresh from the garden, shelled and eaten in a raw or natural state. I use that as an example of the fact that the more we manufacture our foods, the more we refine out the vital minerals and vitamins.
Let us look at another study. Since World War II the consumption of highly refined foods, canned foods, frozen foods, TV dinners as well as food consumed in restaurants has increased extremely rapidly. Along with the acceleration of manufactured food has been a corresponding decrease in the value of nutrients.
As I have said, many chemicals are put into our food. There is the whole area of artificial colouring. An orange is injected with orange dye to make it more orange. Chickens are injected with dye to make them a certain colour. These things are totally unnecessary and scientists are now starting seriously to question them. This practice has only occurred in the last 30, 40 or possibly 50 years. The cumulative effects of many of

these changes are not known in a very concrete or definitive way.
Many Canadians would be surprised to know that the average person consumes over 100 pounds of sugar per year. Not much of that comes out of the sugar bowl; most of it has been added to other foods. There is a lot of medical evidence which indicates that we are eating far too much sugar. It is not good for us. Many breakfast cereals and canned fruits actually contain more sugar than the particular food one is supposedly purchasing.
All these matters are of great concern to me. They are of increasing concern to a larger and larger number of people in Canada and in other countries. In addition to what I have mentioned, there is increasing concern about the safety aspect with regard to the pesticides and insecticides being used. There is growing concern about the hormones given to animals as well as the antibiotics being injected into them. There is concern about forcefeeding of animals in order to fatten them rapidly. There is a lot of concern about how we raise chickens and animals, how we are changing the genetics of some of the animals we eventually eat.
Because of growing evidence that we are so rapidly changing the food system, it would be worth while to put more money into the area of preventive medicine and nutrition. We in this House have often been reminded of escalating health and hospital costs in Canada. Too little attention is being paid to preventive medicine and other ways of bringing down these rapidly escalating costs. None of us have the magic solution. That is why we need a lot more research in this area.
Worth-while research is being done in other countries. Israel, France and Norway all have eating patterns and food different from that in Canada. It is worth taking a look at them. I want to deal with eight or nine points which I feel might improve the health of Canadians.
First, we need a comprehensive educational program. Just the other day I talked to someone who was convinced she eats very well. She consumes three or four cokes a day. Her favourite foods are french fries and macaroni.

speechtext: What's wrong with macaroni?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Anything in a reasonable amount will not harm you. However, if it is your diet for many, many years it will do some harm. Therefore, we need an educational program to inform Canadians about foods they are consuming and those that they should look at more positively.
Second, we should consider a system of nutritional labelling. This has been tried in other countries. People would then know from the label what they are about to consume. The label should indicate the percentage of sugar, fats, cholesterol, solids, and anything else contained in the food.
Another thing that has been suggested by the Canadian Committee on Diet and Cardiovascular Disease is the use of a government logo. The logo would mark foods that are part of a
February 5, 1979

healthy and balanced diet. People would know by the very presence of the logo whether or not what they are consuming is part of a healthy and balanced diet. And here is an idea which could be borrowed from a country like Norway: you could use the taxation system as a way of discriminating in favour of nutritional foods and against foods of non-nutritional value by imposing higher taxes on foods that are unhealthy, lowering the taxes on, and thus lowering the price of, foods which are healthier for people. Norway is experimenting in this direction.
Another thing which could be done, and I thought we had already started to do this in this country, is to subsidize some of the basic foods such as milk and bread. There used to be consumer subsidies on them but they have now been withdrawn.

Powdered milk. It was announced before Christmas that the subsidy on bread would be withdrawn and on January 1 we saw the effect on the price of a loaf of bread in every store in this country. Another thing that could be done is school food programs and school milk programs so that people while they were young would have a chance to eat more nutritious foods in the schools instead of using the classical coke machines and chips, so that children could drink milk and fruit juices and so on in school cafeterias.
Another thing that is very important is the type of advertising beamed at young people. One thing I like that the Quebec government is doing in the area of consumer legislation today is the banning of advertising directed to people under the age of 13. I never used to worry about this until very recently, but I worry about it now because I have a five-year-old son and I see the impact television is making on him and on his preferences. No matter how much we try to tell him that certain breakfast cereals, for example, are not good for him and that other foods such as whole grain cereals are much better for him, we find it hard to convince him because of the fancy ads on television with fancy characters promoting some of the more junky type foods.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Some people say turn off the television, but that is very difficult to do with young people. In the International Year of the Child perhaps one of our concerns should be getting rid of advertising that tries to promote food of nonnutritional value in the mind of a small child. I see a member of the cabinet shaking his head in the negative. I hope he doesn't really mean that, because it is so important in our society that we give the younger people the proper values and the proper type of education so that they will understand the types of foods and the types of values that are good for them in their formative years.
Health Resources Fund Act
These are just a few of the things that I think could be done to improve the health of the nation. That is why when this bill came back to the House for third reading a couple of days ago I wanted to get up and say a few words about what I think is one of the great problems of the industrialized food system and what it is probably doing to our bodies and to our health. It seems to me it is worth putting a few more bucks into this system in terms of the future of our country, because nothing is as important as the health of people. I believe politicians have to take a lead in this area, just as politicians had to take a lead in the area of the delivery of health services, medicare, hospitalization and good hospitals, and modern drugs and technology. We must now start delivering the other half of that formula, which is a good, wholesome food system and a good, balanced diet, along with such things as exercise.
I think that by investing a few million dollars we could reap several billion dollars worth of return, as the health officials to whom I referred have suggested, from the improved health and happiness of the country. Perhaps we could create a much better society for all of us and for those who are about to come in the years ahead.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to enter this debate today as one who represents an area with a large Indian population whose health services really need to be questioned.
The minister proposes to cut some $84 million from science support programs and medical research. During the recent controversy about the reduction in Indian health services we heard frightening statistics on this subject. Indian women in Canada live an average of 30 years less than other women; the life expectancy of Indian men is about 22 years shorter than that of the average Canadian male; the infant mortality rate is twice the national average and natives suffer a much higher incidence of diseases such as tuberculosis and hepatitis.
Perhaps even more startling than today's pathology and mortality figures are reports upon the stature of the North American Indian of yesterday. Many of the facts I am about to put on record were noted in an NIB paper two years ago; I thought it was time they were brought to the attention of the House.
The agricultural Iroquois male of the early 1800s averaged in excess of six feet in height compared to the average European male of that same time standing five feet two inches tall. Infections and chronic disease were unknown in the pre-colonial Americas, while in Europe, during the dark ages, whole populations fell to the ravages of various plagues and diseases. Of 30,000 identified diseases, only 87 were known to exist among the Indian people of the Americas. The difference is attributed to the absence of fresh fruits and vegetables in the European diet and the almost total reliance on dried grains and domesticated meat.
Published studies regarding the Indian people show the race is superior in bodily proportions, colour and gesture; free from tuberculosis, syphilis, and the consequent physical and mental
2888

February 5, 1979
Health Resources Fund Act
deformities. They were strangers to leprosy, scrofula, cancer, and nervous prostration.
Archaeology has failed to uncover evidence among pre-contact Indian burial excavations of modern day bone deficiences, cavities, rheumatism, arthritis, etc. Indian women were unusually strong, often continuing their regular physical activities immediately following childbirth. Infant mortality was rare.
Contact historians of the early eighteenth and nineteenth centuries concur that the Indian people represented a superior physical make-up. Today the Indian people suffer from gall bladder infections, infectious diseases, high infant mortality, obesity, retarded physical growth, and chronic diseases.
The incidence of diabetes among Indians is reported to be five times as high as it is among the general population. A few weeks ago the minister was presented with a blanket by the Union of British Columbia Indian Chiefs with the assurance that it was disease free. The gift was a reference to blankets containing a smallpox virus given to the Ottawa Indians on the upper Great Lakes by British officers 200 years earlier in an attempt to wipe out native settlements. Significant here is that, whether by intent or not, European immigrants introduced along with fatal illnesses the need for the benefits of advanced health care.
Following the confederation of 1867 it was recognized that the federal government should be responsible for Indians and the lands reserved for Indians. While not provided for in the federal statutes, health care services were supplied to Indians, often by surgeons in the Northwest Mounted Police, and by the Hudson's Bay Company. This common practice was first documented by an order in council dated May 11, 1877, appointing Daniel Haggerty, MD as medical superintendent to the Indians of Keewatin and the northwest. Health care services to Indian people over the next century developed gradually, hindered by a changing or non-existent administration and poor organization.
In 1905 Dr. P. Bryce was appointed medical superintendent within the department of Indian affairs. After five years his position was terminated and not reinstated until 1927. At about that time the first field nurses were appointed to work on reserves. However, the general health of the Indian people continued in a downward slide.
The first nursing station ever to be built in the area I represent was built in 1947. At that time it was a case of survival of the fittest. Many Indian people at that time trapped away from their communities. They came back to their communities to buy groceries, to sell their furs and so forth. It would not be unusual to see a family return in the spring with two or three of their children missing, because at that time the Indian people had to depend either on the medicine man or on their knowledge of how to treat a child when it became sick. As nursing stations were built a job had to be performed by the department, and I must give credit to some of the first nurses to come into the northern part of Manitoba-I am sure the same is true in other provinces-because there was a mood
of distrust with regard to the nurses. At that time there were many medicine men who would not accept the fact that there were some who were more powerful than they to treat the sick in various communities, but over a period of time the communities built up a trust for the government's ability to provide health care services.
In 1946 family allowances were introduced, and parents whose children were not attending school could not collect. This brought families closer together. It brought families in from outlying areas to communities in which they were not accustomed to living. They had been accustomed to roaming the land, living in winter camps, trapping, fishing, hunting, selling their furs and raising their families. When the family allowance was introduced, it was compulsory that children attend school. In order to collect family allowances, Indian families had to move into communities. They built log shacks. They began living, not always peacefully, with their next door neighbours and sending their children to school. This happened only 30 years ago, which is a very short time in any country's life.
Then came environmental problems within those communities. The people were not accustomed to living so closely together. There was more money, and as a result there was garbage to contend with. There was no garbage pick-up and no running water. No facilities whatsoever were provided. This is the treatment the Indian people received, and Indian people did not trust the medicine the white man brought in. They did not feel it would be effective in treating very sick people. Medicine men were used extensively just 30 years ago. When we talk about expending to do research on the health of Indian people, we are talking about something which started only 30 years ago. I am sure that some of the studies which began 30 years ago are still ongoing, but they will have to be discontinued because funds are going to be cut off.
In 1945 Indian health services were transferred from the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development to the Department of National Health and Welfare. Important here is the fact that only the administration of the diagnostic and treatment aspects of health services was transferred. Control of environmental health conditions remained under the authority of the Indian affairs department. This is when the Indian affairs department became responsible for the health environment of the Indian people and Indian health services came under another department. In that way the buck could be passed and people could say, "It is not our responsibility; it is up to the other department". I will get into that a little later because we do not have one department taking full responsibility for the health of Indian people in Canada.
In 1962 a further amalgamation took place as Indian health services merged with six other federal health programs to establish the medical services branch, as it is known today. The refinement of Indian health care services to a single branch within the government has done little to help status Indians on reserves. Symptoms are treated, but the causes are left to others.

February 5, 1979

The Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is responsible for the over-all well-being of the Indian people of Canada. In a statement on January 24, 1979, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) said that the basic causes of the poor health of Indian people are socioeconomic; for example, inadequate housing, water supply and sewage disposal, and unemployment. That is true, but only in part, because 1 can cite at least a dozen other examples from the reserves in my constituency.
Just recently I took a two-week extensive trip through the eastern part of my constituency. The Minister of National Health and Welfare visited there last summer. Her visits consisted of dropping into a community, going to the nursing station, having someone meet her to take her out fishing and for a short lunch, coming back, catching the aeroplane and flying on to another community. The minister could then stand up in the House and say that she had visited the communities and that there were no problems. I call it a 24-hour wonder when someone decides to investigate an Indian reserve and 24 hours later comes back with all the information she feels she should have and makes a glowing report. Some people wander in and 24 hours later wander out, and people up there wonder what they really came for.
The minister mentioned the socio-economic aspect. I went to seven reserves which comprise approximately 6,000 people in total. In other parts of the country we have seen school enrolments drop, but in my part of the country enrolment has increased at least threefold over the past seven years. There is not sufficient schoolroom space in many of those communities. Schools that are now only three years old are short of two classrooms. I do not know where the planners were in the various departments, but anyone who had taken the time to look at the statistics and the growth rate in the particular communities could have predicted that more schools would be required. Now, because of the government's restraint program, we see in many communities material which the department had shipped to the community for the purpose of building a school lying there in a heap and not being used because the Treasury Board has cut off further funds to build the additional facilities.
Housing is the number one priority in those communities. I am glad to see the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Faulkner) is leaving the House.

He just cannot face the music, that is all. In many of the communities there are four and five families living in one house. The Minister of National Health and Welfare points to the lack of housing. I am sure there are a dozen people on this side of the House representing Indian communities who could have told the minister that, and who in fact have been telling her that over the past four or five years.
The trouble is that people in the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development have a phobia regarding
Health Resources Fund Act
the only type of housing which they consider is required in northern Manitoba and in isolated areas, namely, a frame house. Some designer has designed a frame house which he considers to be adequate for the Indian people. I could take you, Mr. Speaker, into the homes that I have visited myself personally in Oxford House, Wasagamac, St. Theresa, Garden Hill and Red Sucker Lake. When these houses were built, they were probably built to the standards prescribed by the then minister of Indian affairs and northern development or some of his officials. These houses are not equipped with running water or with other modern facilities such as a hot water tank. In the winter time, when three or four families live in one house, there are at least two or three tubs of water sitting on the stove in order to heat water for the occupants. This generates massive amounts of condensation which in turn frosts up the windows and the doors, to the extent that neither can be opened. The neighbour, if he can get out of his own house, has to come in and open the door in the morning. There are no doorknobs left in most of those homes. There is a piece of rope attached through a hole in the door, and you have to haul on that to open the door. Until such time as these homes in the north are equipped to provide running water, the people there may as well go back to the conventional log home.
In many of the communities I visited people are saying they will rebel and ask the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development to put a log housing program back into operation. They claim that their children were far healthier when they lived in log homes than they are in the sweat boxes in which they have to live today. All you have to do is to talk to the nurses at the various nursing stations. They do a wonderful job but they will tell you how frustrating it is for them at times when they see the idiotic approach taken by the Minister of National Health and Welfare cutting back on certain facilities and services in those communities.
