Mr. Speaker, particularly relating to measures dealing with health, the government of the day may become known as the halfway house

government, because historically it has undertaken programs which seem to reflect the philosophy of the Liberal party, and at a time such as this it has decided to withdraw. It has withdrawn at a time when the objectives of the policies have not been achieved in full. This is a very retrograde step to take. The government made commitments through the Department of National Health and Welfare respecting the improvement of teaching and treatment facilities, but it has withdrawn before they were completed. Perhaps this is as critical a point in the program covered by the act as any and the step taken by the government is one which is inexcusable and unforgiveable.
Every now and then in the life of a politician there comes a point when one finds himself or herself to be a pawn of the circumstances of the day. Certainly the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) finds herself in the unenviable position of being a pawn of the government which cuts back on its promises to Canadians, particularly as they relate to health.
This proposed cutback will build in regional disparities by withdrawing from or reducing programs which were intended to arrest the difficulties in the less fortunate areas of Canada. In particular, the proposal will extend the disparities the government has professed it will cure. It is rather peculiar to watch the expenditures of government as it looks at what is political and how to gain votes. As mentioned by the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Smith), the government will build arenas but cuts back on health. It is hard to follow the logic of that type of political philosophy. While the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) (Mrs. Campagnolo) may be sitting on the pedestal at this moment in time, the Minister of National Health and Welfare is subject to criticisms of the severest kind which can be levelled at a politician.
I regret very much the transfer of moneys from one field to another, particularly when the job is not complete as the moneys are transferred. There is no indication the government is prepared to honour the projects presently under way by extending federal aid to the provinces. For instance, a project in the city of Saint John was to be financed partly by the federal government. Yet there has been no assurance in writing to the minister of health of New Brunswick as of noon today that the federal government in fact will honour its commitment to this ongoing project. I suppose we will see government members from New Brunswick rise in support of the bill, in spite of the fact that there is no assurance that present commitments will be honoured and that moneys in fact will be advanced.
There were two further projects in the province of New Brunswick which anticipated assistance through the government's program in order to provide better teaching and more intensive care facilities in areas where they do not exist. At the present time the people in those areas are doing the best they can with the available facilities. In the cities of Edmundston and Campbellton two projects were on the drawing board which were to be built with the aid of the program during its term. These projects would have provided better health care within two federal Liberal constituencies in the province of

New Brunswick, but federal government assistance has been withdrawn.
There is very little excuse for extending the disparities which exist in health care in the less favoured provinces, as this proposal will do. This is but one example of the inequities which exist in the less favoured areas of Canada. Extended health care is assisted by the federal government on the basis of $20 per capita. Perhaps that does not mean much to Alberta and British Columbia, and perhaps it is not necessary in either case; but $20 per capita in the less favoured provinces is not enough to help them extend their levels of care to those of the more favoured provinces.
I do not wish to carry this to the ridiculous, but it goes without saying that the larger centres always will have the best care of any centres in Canada. That is by virtue of the opportunities for health officials, doctors and nurses to practise in specialty fields, which opportunities cannot be provided in smaller communities. Perhaps there will be only half a dozen major centres in Canada where maximum care can be extended in health; but there are hundreds of communities which need to come a little closer to the level of the greater centres. There was a step which aided them in doing so, but now it is to be withdrawn. At least two projects in New Brunswick will not be favoured with the assistance offered by the program.
The government's proposal contradicts totally the concept of long-term planning for health care. As I am not a medical doctor, I will not try to infringe upon the medical field by suggesting specific methods of extending health care, but as a member of the House I am interested in equality of care. This present step by the govenment will constrict the opportunity for equality in the less favoured areas of Canada, as will practically all programs which presently are being cut back. These will be known as the "Begin years" in health, when the Government of Canada practised austerity by withdrawing some of its support from medical, hospital care, extended care services and educational facilities. subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF IMPROVING VIABILITY OF INDUSTRY
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of taking the appropriate steps to make agriculture a more viable industry in Canada.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity of discussing in this House a problem which is near and dear to the hearts of the many of us who sit here as representatives of rural ridings. We know that in spite of the great admiration the current federal agriculture minister has for himself and for his abilities, which he has expressed on many occasions in this House, agriculture in this country is indeed having great difficulty. As a result farmers are moving off the land in ever-increasing numbers.
To illustrate the problem briefly, it seems to boil down to one of constantly falling income and constantly increasing costs. The problem can be well illustrated in terms of income. The average farm in this country, particularly in the west, involves a total capital investment in the area of $173,000, including land, machinery, equipment and all those things required to conduct a farming operation. If one were to take that $173,000 in cash and invest it in a savings account, or perhaps in bonds, one could reasonably expect to gain a return of at least 10 per cent. This would mean an expected income from this size of deposit of somewhere in the neighbourhood of $17,300. The fact is that the net income from a farm with a

February 5, 1979
Agriculture
capital outlay of this size is nowhere near the income that could be derived from an investment of that money directly in a savings account of a long-term nature. As a matter of fact, my calculations indicate that the average farm I have described would produce a net income of somewhere between $13,000 and $14,000.
We have a situation in which a man engaged in agriculture in this country not only does not get paid for his work, but he loses money on his investment since he could do better in terms of return by simply taking the money out of farming and putting it into a savings account of some sort.
The result of this situation has been a mass exodus of people in rural areas from farms into the cities, with a subtantial rural depopulation and the destruction of many small towns which dry up when these people move away. Indeed, this has resulted in the destruction of a lifestyle which many Canadians have enjoyed in the past.
The situation has reached the point where virtually no one is entering agriculture, particularly young farmers, because prospects for a reasonable income are poor. If a young man does decide to farm, the capital required is so great that he must borrow a huge amount of money, and he finds it virtually impossible to meet the cost of servicing that sort of loan. As a result, most of these young people must spend nearly half their time, usually in the winter months, working elsewhere at some other type of employment simply to keep the farm running. It seems to me there is something wrong with a system under which that can happen. It is not right that a young farmer who undertakes an operation with an investment of $173,000 must get a job in the oil fields or somewhere else simply in order to stay in the business of farming.
When we examine that situation we see there is something terribly wrong with the policies this government has been following. In my view there are two main things that should be considered and studied if some kind of corrective action is to take place. Steps must be taken to increase gross income to the farmer. On the other side of the coin, something needs to be done to reduce the cost of operation: that is, the cost of machinery, fuel, repair parts, farm labour and so on.
Let me come to the key question posed by this motion. Given the facts I have already laid out, is agriculture really a viable industry? We know that world consumption of food and feed grains has continued to grow on the average 5 per cent per year. If we compound this rate we will see that in 15 years consumption will double. When we look at growth in production in this country we will see that it will not nearly keep up with this expected increase in demand.
The Canadian cattle industry lost more than $400 million in the last four years, and much of this loss can be reflected in the decrease in producer equity of some 18 per cent. In other words, because the beef industry was in such dire straits in terms of low prices, 18 per cent of herds have been sold off, resulting in a shortage even greater than we anticipated. If these herds are to be rebuilt it is essential that producers have confidence not only that the market recovery which is now

being enjoyed to some extent remains permanent, but also that the government will not act to frustrate that recovery.
All Canadian producers will remember the action of the Canadian government in 1976 when huge quantities of offshore beef came into our market and seriously depressed Canadian cattle prices. This created major problems in respect of our relations with our neighbours, and certainly major problems for the beef industry.
I recall very clearly the minister standing in this House at the time complaining that there was overproduction, that we had a huge surplus of beef, and asking farmers to cut production as that was the only way to improve prices. What he neglected to say at that time was that the huge surplus we supposedly has was largely the result of huge imports from offshore sources. If we examine the figures in respect to our own production very carefully, even during those years when we had this supposed surplus we will see that our production was not sufficient during any of those years to meet Canada's own demand.
The other question I want to touch upon is what can be done to resolve the situation. After all, the motion does say that the government must take steps to make agriculture more viable, so clearly it is necessary to make some recommendations as to how this can be done.
To begin with, some changes in the tax system are required to make it more equitable. Trade and economic policies must be adjusted so that Canadian agriculture is capable of competing efficiently in both world and domestic markets in respect of the commodities we produce. Government policies must be aimed at maximizing our competitive position and extending our markets, rather than what seems to have become the general trend of this government, simply to be satisfied with bringing forward government support and supply management programs.
In looking at the situation in the long term, it seems to me that support subsidies and supply management are at best short-term solutions and that the long-term solutions must rest on improving efficiency, expanding the market and stabilizing prices through these expanded and reasonable markets.
There have been problems with regard to offshore trade policies. I have already mentioned that too much beef has been brought in, the result of which has caused the artificial depression of our own prices. We on this side of the House have suggested, to avoid this difficulty in the future, that a longterm beef import policy be instituted to protect the producers from artificial world surplus and competition from other products.
There have been problems with regard to grain and they are partially due to the fact that the international grain arrangement has expired. We are carrying on negotiations, but at the moment grains are at the mercy of market forces and as a result prices are not what they could be. There should be greater effort on the part of this government to reinstate the international grain arrangement that would guarantee the
February 5, 1979

maintenance of a reasonable floor for prices of exported grains.
The biggest problem which needs to be studied very carefully and corrected, and regarding which the government has shown great neglect, is transportation. We must take steps to ensure the adequacy of grain transportation and handling, that the cost of transporting grain remains at a reasonable level, and that the structure of the handling industry itself adjusts to function with greatest efficiency.
There has been a suggestion on the part of the government that the Crowsnest pass rates may be changed. If one looks at the history of this government, one becomes very frightened that these changes which they are talking about will only further depress farm income. We want to make sure that if the Crowsnest pass rates are changed, such changes will reflect compensation to the railways for their work and that these compensatory costs will not be borne by the producers but by the government from its general revenue.
Another problem in the area of grain handling is strikes. There have been occasions over the past decade and perhaps even longer when ships from other countries have come to our ports to be loaded, but because of strikes and poor transportation policies they have waited for days and days, incurring demurrage charges of approximately $5,000 per day per ship. All these costs are pawned off on the producer of grain.
The result of this inefficient grain handling system has been that Canada's share of world markets for wheat has dropped from 24 per cent to 14 per cent, while the United States, with its more efficient handling system and vigorous marketing efforts, has increased its share from 38 per cent to 41 per cent. Clearly, this is an area of great importance to Canada, and we all look to this government to take some action to ensure that labour disputes in the grain handling industry be settled in a reasonable way.
My party has suggested that it is time we re-examine the old strike weapon, particularly in areas of essential services, which includes railway transportation and grain handling, and that it be replaced by a body that we have named the public interest disputes commission. The powers of that body would be either to settle a dispute or, at least, to facilitate negotiations toward an agreeable settlement. In either case, something is required beyond what we are currently experiencing that would have the effect of smoothing out the business of grain handling and delivery.
There are other members who have indicated a desire to speak on this very important issue, and since we have only an hour for private members' business I would like to conclude by saying that agriculture is a large business which requires the concentrated efforts of governments at all levels and the concentrated attention of all the institutions involved in transport, production, marketing and distribution of agricultural products. Concentrated attention is required toward keeping our producers in business and maintaining a high quality of product to feed the people of this country.
Agriculture
As I mentioned earlier, we have an aging population in the rural areas and fewer people are going into farming. The danger in the long term is that there will be fewer and fewer producers and, therefore, we will not be able to produce enough to feed our people, making us more and more dependent on imports for our food supply. Given the volatile situations which arise in the world from time to time, it seems to me that a government that has a policy of becoming more and more dependent on other countries for our food supply is not looking after the best interests of this country.
We have two choices, and they are these. Either this government takes action to ensure that we continue to do what Canada does best-to grow food in such a way that those involved in the industry will be adequately compensated for their labours-or, if it fails to do that, the only possible alternative which will assure Canada of a long-term food supply is to replace this lazy government. I suggest that the latter is the only solution to this problem from a long-term point of view.

subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF IMPROVING VIABILITY OF INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words on this very important motion before us. The hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) has called on the government to make agriculture more viable through its policies. My main concern is that unless there are radical changes in the government's agricultural policy, our country will not be by the year 2000 self-sufficient in producing our own needs. That statement was made recently by the Science Council of Canada and is rather shocking in view of the fact that food and agriculture represent $30 billion to this country each year.
Agriculture is our most important industry and a very important part of this country. We must put more stress and emphasis on the food and agriculture system. If we continue as we are now, the day will come when this country will be a net importer of food. Even more shocking is the fact that if we take away the grains and oil seeds which are produced in such great abundance in western Canada, we are already a net importer of food. For example if we eliminate grains and oil seeds from last year's agricultural income, we were a net importer of food into our country in the amount of $1.8 billion. This is a very shocking indictment of the government which sits across the way in terms of its lack of planning in the food and agriculture industry of our nation.
Let us now look at a few statistics which I think are absolutely startling. We are a large country with a relatively small population. If we had planned our food production well we should be producing enough food to feed not only ourselves but other people around the world.
Only 4 per cent of Canada's vast land area is arable land, Mr. Speaker. We have about 460 million acres which can be farmed of which around 104 million acres are under cultivation. This is where things get frightening. We find that through a lack of government policy a lot of that farm land is being paved. We are losing some 250 acres of prime agricul-

February 5, 1979
Agriculture
ture land per day to factories, highways, housing developments. 1 understand that the Department of Fisheries and the Environment has federal land use policy under consideration, and I hope this is true. During the past year we have asked the minister many questions about a federal land use program that, with the provinces, would reserve food land for the production of food and that would encourage industrial development on land that cannot produce food. We understand that a policy directive to that effect is being produced. I hope it is a tough policy that will make sure we preserve food land for the production of food.
One of the tragedies of this country is that cities such as Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver are located on the best agricultural land. Once land is paved over it cannot be reclaimed. Once there is a housing development, an expressway, a city park or anything on it, the land cannot be reclaimed. I do not think that makes any sense whatsoever. There are many places in Canada where factories and developments could be placed-sites not far from Montreal or Toronto on land that is not fit for farming. If it were used for this purpose, then the food land could be reserved for the production of food.
The only government to do anything important in this area is the government of British Columbia under the former premier, Mr. Barrett. It introduced a bill four or five years ago that reserved food land for the production of food. A similar approach is being considered in Quebec. I think the federal government should act in this area because there is a lot of land controlled by the federal government that could be rezoned. Cost-sharing plans could be introduced to entice provinces to put away food land for the production of food. These things should be done if we are to have a more viable agriculture industry.
We know that when urban population doubles the amount of arable land is reduced by one third. Today we are importing foods that we should not be importing. I am not talking of growing cucumbers in snowbanks, as the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) once spoke about; I am talking about self-sufficiency in such basic things as beef. We produce only about 94 per cent of the beef we consume, and there really is no reason why we could not produce it all.
There are many other products in which we are not self-sufficient, such as broilers. About a year ago the Agricultural Research Institute of Canada said that because of the tremendous importation of chickens the gross economic loss to Canada in 1977 was over $100 million. Mr. Speaker, that means jobs on the farm, in the handling and processing of eggs and food in general. Money could be saved or generated if this commodity was produced in our own country. There would be a positive effect on the balance of trade and on the Canadian dollar. These are reasons why we must strive toward greater food self-sufficiency.
1 should like to suggest that we should use a lot of our waste heat and energy to heat huge greenhouses that would produce a lot more fruit and vegetables. So much of what we consume

comes from the United States and elsewhere when it should really be produced in Canada.
In a nutshell, Mr. Speaker, I believe that if we do not begin preserving farm land for the production of food, if we do not plan the agricultural sector better, if we do not start encouraging farmers to produce food at a stable price then even if we include grain and oil seeds this country will not be self-sufficient by the year 2000, as the Science Council of Canada has said.
My second concern is that the farmer is receiving less and less of the food dollar. About 25 years ago the farmer received around 60 per cent of the food dollar, but today he receives slightly under 40 per cent. More and more of the food dollar is going to the large wholesalers, retailers and processors-to the middlemen who process, manufacture, package and transport the food. This is a matter which should be of great concern not only to farmers but also to consumers, especially when you look at the rapidly escalating price of food-19'/2 per cent in 1978. The middle man receives the greatest share of that increase.
Questions were asked in the House today about the escalating price of beef. All of us know that the farmer deserves a greater return for his cattle. For three or four years cattle prices have been poor. When the price of beef went up on Friday by 18 per cent at the stockyards, it was predicted that by today or tomorrow supermarket prices would increase by 10 per cent and shortly by another 8 per cent. I question why this should happen so quickly when they are using old inventory beef from their lockers. The farmers and the consumers are concerned about such things as the power of the middleman, in this case the supermarkets and packing plants, to manipulate prices.
Recently when CSIP issued a report showing that profits in the food and beverage industry had gone up by 63 per cent in the last year, consumers were, of course, scandalized. I think farmers and consumers have found a common villain-the middleman who all too often is taking too large a share of the food dollar. This is an area the government should be looking into.
My third and final concern is transportation. I see the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) in the House making notes. I hope he will rise to utter a few graceful words on this subject.
The transportation system in this country is a national joke, as is borne out in statistics issued recently by the Canadian Wheat Board. These show that because of a lack of boxcars and because of deficiencies in the railway system in this country, we have lost sales amounting to $230 million. There is no excuse for this, Mr. Speaker. There is no reason why we cannot have a proper rail system, a good delivery system and enough boxcars to transport the grain to market.
We speak of national unity, of a new constitution and priorities for the country. I see transportation as a key to uniting the nation so that all parts of the country have equal access to trade and equal opportunities for development. It
February 5, 1979

often makes westerners angry when they consider the discrepancy in freight rates in the country. Cattle can be shipped from Saskatchewan to Toronto on a pound per pound basis cheaper than the processed meat can be shipped. When that is done, the jobs and the money for the processing and slaughtering of the cattle are in Toronto and other parts of southern Ontario. It should be done closer to the source of the product, in this case western Canada. It is because of things like this that Canadians feel alienated and cynical, not just toward the federal government, but to our whole system today. This may not seem important to some people, but it is very important to the beef producer.
The national unity debate is an opportunity to make agriculture more viable and to make our transportation system more equitable for all Canadians.
These are a few of the concerns I have as a westerner in terms of making agriculture more viable and ensuring that we are self-sufficient in food. We will not be if we do not change some of the government policies.
The government must be a lot tougher on the middle man who is ripping off both the consumer and the producer, taking a greater and greater share of the food dollar. As I said about an hour ago in the House, he is radically changing the whole food system in terms of our safety. It is terrifying.
Finally, transportation must be a tool for national development and national unity. It must work on behalf of everyone so that what the farmer produces is processed, developed, packaged and so on as close as possible to the source. In the case of beef, this should be in western Canada. In the case of dairy farming, it should be in places like Quebec and eastern Ontario. The same should apply to fruits and vegetables. These are matters to which we must address ourselves if we are to make agriculture more viable.
Another item for the future is escalating energy costs which are radically changing farming in this country. These might reverse the move from larger and larger more capital and energy-intensive farms to the smaller, more efficient and, in my opinion, more desirable farms. We must look at the cost of energy. It was brought to my attention last week by the Agriculture Institute of Canada that there is not a single person in the Department of Agriculture who co-ordinates energy policy or energy research as it pertains to agriculture. That is one problem the government should correct. It may save this country millions of dollars in the years ahead.
A lot of experiments are being conducted with regard to alternatives on the farm, energy, using some of the waste heat, recycling by-products, the whole question of biomass and so on. More research has to be done and the government should look into this.
If the farmer could be guaranteed a basic standard of living or income, he would produce the food. It is very frustrating to the farmer not to know what his income will be in the months ahead. When he begins to raise a calf in the spring, he does not know what it will sell for in the fall. The same is true of hogs
Agriculture
and other commodities. It depends on the world climate, international markets, the stock exchange and so on. That is what dictates the price for his animal.
I maintain that if we make it a national priority to guarantee the price of commodities to the farmer within certain realistic variations, the farmer would produce food. The consumer at the other end of the food chain would pay a consistent price for the product in the supermarket. One need only compare two commodities, beef and eggs.
This government has done a very good job in terms of guaranteeing a constant supply of eggs through the National Egg Marketing Board. The producer is guaranteed a constant price. On the other side, the consumer pays a stable price for eggs, a price no higher and usually lower than that in the United states.
When it comes to beef, it is the exact opposite. The producer never knows what he is going to get for his livestock. There are tremendous fluctuations in the price the producer receives and what the consumer pays. This is bad for both sides.
A few years ago there was an over-supply of cattle. The price went away down. That is the law of supply and demand. Part of the problem was that the government opened up the borders and allowed beef to come in from the United States, New Zealand and Argentina. The farmers did what they had to do. They sold their herds. They got rid of their cows and did not save their calves. What is happening now is a logical extension of that. There is now a shortage of beef in this country. The price is going up. I maintain that is because there is no planning in that industry as in other food industries, such as eggs.
It is necessary to increase our imports. Prices will go up even more. Most economists say we can expect higher beef prices for the next three or four years. Beef is not like poultry or even like hogs. You cannot get into and out of the cycle quickly. It takes a long time to build up a herd. Most cows have one calf a year.
The situation is not like that with chickens. The chicken in the supermarket freezer is probably only 60 or 70 days old. That is how quickly you can produce a chicken. If there is a shortage of chickens, you merely turn on the tap and in a matter of a few months you have remedied the problem. It is possible to regulate the supply. However, this cannot be done quickly with cattle. That is why we need more planning in that sector for both the farmer and the consumer.
I commend the hon. member for Athabasca for introducing this motion and giving us an opportunity to talk about the reasons why agriculture must be more viable. In the final analysis, it is the backbone of this country from coast to coast.

I should also like to tell him that we on this side share his concerns; if unanimity can be achieved we may even be able to give our Canadian agricultural producers the income they need and are entitled to.
As for the viability of agriculture, Mr. Speaker, we can and must speak of it. That is why I congratulate the hon. member for having brought up the matter today; we are that much more concerned about the producer's income that at this time we have reason to express certain doubts about the conditions under which our producers operate; unfortunately, to speak of the viability of agriculture is too often to speak of the industry and forget the producer.
Firstly and importantly, the motion gives us an opportunity to make this House aware of the need to look at the farmer's real income instead of referring to figures and statistics that, because of increases, are very seldom relevant at the individual producer's level.
Second, the motion also provides us with an opportunity to refer both to the need for and dangers of marketing boards in the face of current difficulties. Third, the motion gives an opportunity to deal with the problems faced by young farmers, and this is of tremendous significance because our young farmers are now incapable of meeting today's challenge without support from the government and various farming organizations.
Fourth, this motion could also give us an opportunity to refer to a commitment, not only from this House in a non-partisan effort, but also from our partners at the farming industry level as a whole, because in agriculture perhaps more than in any other industry it is extremely important that everyone understand and assume his responsibilities when the time comes, so that we may collectively support our Canadian farming industry.
In the course of my remarks I will come back a number of times to the dairy policy, because I for one am somewhat disappointed that the dairy producer, usually small and old, apparently is a victim we are unable to protect within the prevailing system. It therefore seems important on the occasion of a motion on farming viability that we be able to address the dilemma we are now placed in by a mechanism that certainly is inadequate to ensure justice to all producers. The motion gives us an opportunity to recall and expose that situation once more, because small dairy producers in particular are victimized.
Mr. Speaker, I mean tampering with the quotas of some producers at the expense of other producers. We know that in 1976 unfair cuts resulted from this, but what becomes even more unfair is that this situation is perpetuated with the complicity of that system.
Mr. Speaker, I also wish to denounce something else, the fact that in some cases the regulations of some marketing boards are not adequate to protect individual producers efficiently. For instance, if you refer to our dairy policy, the family farm is too often threatened. Older producers are too often the victims of injustice and forced to give up when they worked most of their lives on the farm. Yet, Mr. Speaker, we know that those injustices are part of the system and that, unfortunately, the conflict of interest at the level of some officials and some producers themselves prevents anyone from attempting to correct the situation.
We asked many for the publication of milk quotas. Of course, as you know, it was always rejected. There is probably some valid reasons for this but some of them are still unknown and I hope that some day they will be given to us. I for one would be tempted to launch an inquiry on the distribution and administration of some dairy marketing boards and I hope that if those charges can be made it will give us an opportunity to throw light on this issue and to put an end to this injustice towards small and older producers that we must witness without being able to do anything.
Mr. Speaker, let me come back to the question of farming income. I do not think that in 1979 farm producers have a fair income. We should revise the system in recognizing, as a first priority, not the concerns of the industry but the producers' income. In fact, we are over-specializing agriculture at the expense of the small and the older producer. I do not think we have the right to do that because until the last few years Canadian agriculture has been based on our farmers who, through the force of circumstances, were small and who, quite naturally, have aged, but who are still entitled to keep on working in that sector of activity if they so wish.
Agriculture is no longer a business best left to experts and economists, a thing that is managed in backroom talks. It is first and foremost the farmer's business and he must be understood and compensated fairly with an adequate and even interesting income. As far as marketing boards are concerned,
I think that we and the majority of hon. members must acknowledge that they have a raison d'etre, that they are valuable instruments which we should endeavour to improve. But they should serve the consumer and the producer as well.
But it is time that their applicability to the various agricultural productions be recognized because I do not think that we should stabilize some sectors, which would become privileged agricultural sectors, while producers in other sectors must fight desperately to find a place in our economic system. That is why, Mr. Speaker, I believe we should set up marketing boards as quickly as possible for all types of productions, which will actually serve the interests of producers.
However, Mr. Speaker, the government must always bear in mind its responsibilities towards these boards. I would like, at this point, to examine our responsibilities regarding the

Canadian dairy policy. We are fully aware of the conflicts of interest and the bickering going on over the instruments of our dairy policy, however, the government has unfortunately delegated its responsibilities to certains bodies and by doing so has become powerless in the face of certain cases of injustice.
Third, viability is synonymous with continuity. Personally, that was my first objective when I started out in politics, to ensure continuity and a harmonious resurgence in agriculture with our young people who are capable, who can become competent and who have enough courage to hang on and bring agriculture in the modern era. Naturally I had to set this concern aside temporarily because we had to concentrate, and I think that it is still the case today, on establishing marketing boards and solving all the internal workings problem so that the boards could be operative and efficient. Modern agriculture is a business with modern rules which does not tolerate trial and error. It will never again be what it was, and that is an important thing to understand in order to respond appropriately. It must be allowed to become what it should be.
Fourth, we must recall what our responsibilities are and remember that as partners in the Canadian agricultural industry we have a role to play and that role must be played at the right time and in the right place. Thus each one of us has, in his own field, to review his own responsibilities, and each one of the partners must become more knowledgeable, more competent and no less responsible. Because the success of a farm business depends on the capacity of the partners to work together in the sense of farm economy and of the farmers' income, and at the same time to satisfy the consumers.
That is the new challenge of the day and of the near and more or less distant future.
A perfect illustration of the dilemma that I have put, as regards the income of marketing corporations and the respon-sibilites shared by the partners in the industry, is the national dairy policy, as we all know. And the last annual meeting of the dairy farmers of Canada showed us that on the whole the Canadian industry is doing well. But on the farms, everyday we meet producers who would need higher quotas and who frequently, in the past and even now, are penalized for overproduction. During that period prices for quotas went higher and higher. Three years ago you could buy quotas for $1.37 a hundred weight. Today you have to pay $14, $16, $20, $22 a hundredweight. I for one am prepared to ask the government to take back those responsibilities because it is responsible for the well-being of producers and individuals.
As far as the national dairy policy is concerned, regulations should be the same for everybody and the protection should be effective for all, provided however the protection of small producers is ensured and guaranteed first. The question is: Who can and must protect small producers under the present Canadian dairy policy? Who has that responsibility? Who has the necessary capabilities? The answer is quite simple but at the producer's level, as among people generally speaking, they

are not well informed. The solution, Mr. Speaker, lies in marketing boards or federations of producers. However, in Quebec only the Agricultural Producers' Union could require the federations of whole milk or industrial milk to do so as they are always facing conflicts of interest.
For its part, the federal government cannot do anything because it transferred that power and responsibility, I should say, to provincial agencies at their request. Certainly the Agricultural Producers' Union can do what it wants but for my part, I cannot let small producers disappear without trying to do everything I can or to ask the producers' union to agree to do so, something which I think is advisable for the APU and for producers, or ask the federal government to take upon itself to do so when it has abolished the supply management committee and to take control again probably by subsidy quotas.

In other words, they should not try to do anything if issues are not definitely settled.
As a member who sees what happens in the milk sector, I want people to understand in what kind of situation any hon. member is placed. First it must be said that the administration and the distribution of quotas is the sole responsibility of the federations at the present time. It is a fact which should be recognized. The only responsibility of the federal government or of the Canadian Dairy Commission or of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) is to define Canadian needs and tailor production to demand. As a matter of fact, it is up to the producers, or their representatives, or the supply management committee, or their own federation of whole or industrial milk, or by extension to the Agricultural Producers' Union to distribute the quotas among the farmers.

Mr. Speaker, the move to withdraw from participation in a program recognized as needed by both the federal and provincial jurisdictions reminds one of the land registration and identification program which was undertaken jointly by the Government of Canada and the maritime provinces. That program was evaluated by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and the various provincial governments of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. They studied how land registration problems could be solved, and a program was undertaken. It was agreed each province could afford only so much money on a per annum basis. It was agreed the federal government only wanted to expend a certain fixed amount of money on a per annum basis.
The program was set down for ten years. The expertise and administration structures were assembled. The co-operation between federal and provincial authorities was effected, and the program was under way in a very progressive fashion. It would have placed the maritime provinces in a land registration program which was second to none. As a matter of fact, in the early years of its planning it was examined by several foreign jurisdictions which were somewhat in a bind and needed a comparable or new program.
As was the case in many other financial situations which the government pushed itself into, it chose to withdraw, to limit

the available funds, to constrict the program, and virtually to waste the initial years in which much value had been accumulated. If the program is to be completed, it will be completed by the provinces doing their work under a much retarded program during a period of time when the complete program was required.
In the field of health, again the federal government has failed to predict its capabilities. It has failed to estimate properly the amounts of money required for various programs, and to project them in budget fashion far enough ahead to obtain the correct expenditures in the correct years without a breach of promise. Like so many other things, this is breach of promise by a government which has put itself in its own bind.
One can recall the repeated speeches of all opposition parties in the House. They were critical of the government's failure to predict its requirements two years, three years, four years or five years ahead. The government would not put those requirements on the table. If it had put the requirements on the table five years ago and projected to this point in time, one would find that the provinces which share the cost would not be in the embarrassing positions in which they now find themselves. The provinces could have projected their requirements and spread the money out. It could have been done in a manner so that all provinces would have received the benefits of the programs under health and land registration services which are now being cut. This is another example of where the provinces are being used as the guinea pigs of politics by the government.
This afternoon we heard an answer in the House by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) in reply to a proper request pertaining to health. She indicated that we should speak to our provincial ministers of health, as if there was no responsibility of the Government of Canada in a cost-shared program. That is not the case, because the guidelines are laid down. If a province is not operating as the federal government wishes it to, then the federal government lowers the boom and withdraws money. But when a province wants out, then the Minister of National Health and Welfare says, "Speak to your provincial minister." It is an iniquitous transfer of political responsibility to others who have no control over the situation.
When the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Buchanan) pulls the puckering string on the purse, the money no longer goes to the provinces, and the provinces must answer to the people. They are the ones who receive the direct blame. It does not make any difference whether it is Ontario or New Brunswick; it constricts provincial programs and planning. This is not in line with any program which is intended to create a unified Canada. It is a continuous confrontation with one provincial minister after another because of the retraction of a position which was in place. It is a reflection upon the absolute need for long-term planning and commitment which Canada can recognize as a promise to be fulfilled and not withdrawn.
If we were to look for promises which have been withdrawn,
I suppose we would not have to go very far. We could go back to the Department of Transport release of last week. We would

see that while money is being withdrawn from health programs, the government recognizes the political requirements of certain ports in the country and has promised Newfoundlanders a synchrolift in St. John's, for the second time. I wonder if they will get a synchrolift. It was promised in the past, and obviously it is an election promise at this time. Also the government has broken its promise of a synchrolift for Newfoundland. There is a great deal to be accomplished in health. I cannot hope to compete with the medical group who have spoken on this matter, such as the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) and others. As a member from a small town, I understand the difficulties small communities have in obtaining doctors. At this point in time it is ill-advised for the government to withdraw anything from the health program because such action further discourages doctors to move into some of the smaller communities. It puts the facilities the program would have bought farther away from those small villages than they otherwise would have been.
The program was undertaken with the idea of first building the most important health centres in the provinces concerned. As soon as the major centres were served, then it was planned to look at the outlying ones. This was not because health care was any less important in more distant points. It was because it was imperative that the capability be in place, province by province, and extended as fast as possible to as many communities as possible. The maritime provinces are faced with an uncompleted program, one which must be completed in due time but at a slower rate than otherwise planned. Once again smaller communities around the country will find it more difficult as time goes on, because of the slowdown in the supply of services which they so badly require to look after their health needs.
Perhaps this is the price of federal mismanagement which is being paid by the communities and provinces of Canada. It was a poor estimate of the general cost of government down the line. It is another example of the government's effort at so-called austerity. It is coupled with the withdrawal of moneys from Indian health services and the proposal to reduce payments for hospitals and medicare. It is a high profile program of federal government expenditure. It is intended to illustrate to Canadians as a whole that they may not want federal government austerity. The emphasis placed by austerity on health research in general indicates that the government
Health Resources Fund Act
is looking for complaints from the public about austerity and trying to say, "There, I told you the people do not want austerity after all. They do not want it at all, they only think they want austerity." That is far from the truth.
We have a program which is being cancelled two years before its proper date, and it is being cancelled without prior consultation with the ministers of health in the provinces concerned. As I said earlier in my remarks, it has been cancelled without any assurance or firm commitment that the projects presently under way will in fact get the money which the provinces thought was committed because this little bird was cut off so close behind the ears even the payments which are committed are not assured to the ministers.
There is no question but that the provinces concerned will have to proceed with the programs which were intended; the buildings, the facilities, and care services, because the provinces in good faith have extended the assurance to these various communities that in year one, two, or three, the facilities they require will be built in co-operation with the federal government. These statements have been made by the provinces in Canada, but now the provinces will have to go back and say that because of the withdrawal of federal funds they will have to move these projects down to year one plus one, year two plus two, and year three plus three. They will apologize, but follow up by saying that this is not too far away. This is a transfer of political liability, political responsibility and political blame, not just to New Brunswick, but to every province in Canada that was trying to improve its extended care and educational facilities in the health field.
We have to look at this from a national point of view and on a national basis. I have tried to do that. I will admit that it is my resonsibility to represent New Brunswick, and I do that to the best of my ability, but not without having a conception in respect of the national impact of all these things.
What this means is that Campbellton will be a little later in getting the facilities which the province of New Brunswick had planned for that city; that Edmundston will be a little later than it had planned in receiving its facilities and services; and that the city of Saint John in the province of New Brunswick will not know whether the federal government's commitments will be kept for the construction of facilities and services already planned with moneys already committed by the provincial treasurer. In this case I happen to know whereof I speak, and I am sure that such a situation is not unique to one province in Canada as this applies on a national basis.
No one is any more anxious than I to see this government cut down on its expenditures, but what I want to see from this government is one single, really sincere effort to cut a low profile item rather than a high profile one, proving to this nation that austerity is its objective, rather than proving to Canada that austerity is unacceptable, which is its present objective. This is totally unacceptable as a program of government under any guise.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to take part in the debate on Bill C-2. Even though it looks quite weak and simplistic, this bill holds some unpleasant surprises in the general area of public health care. Mr. Speaker, the health resources fund, which was created in 1966, will normally be of use to public health care for another two years. However, this government has gotten into the habit in a time of peace and abundance, or at least of so-called abundance, to hack away at expenditures. Unfortunately, it does not cut back on extravagant or useless expenditures, it prefers to cut back on useful and essential expenditures, especially as concerns health care for the Canadian population.
Health is a great gift, Mr. Speaker. It is the greatest of gifts for all mankind. We jealously protect the health of animals and ecological systems, but unfortunately, when it comes to the health of our fellow citizens, we have a tendency to put health aside to save money. Under the circumstances, Mr. Speaker, this has become a real paranoia because certain programs which are well-designed and essential for our welfare will suffer.
The Minister believes that the health resources fund, which was created to provide assistance to the laboratories and the necessary facilities to train medical and health care personnel, must be abolished. In her wisdom, she has thought up this idea. Already, in the sixties, it had become necessary to improve all health services and their availability. Indeed, this has always been necessary. The government had taken the leadership in this field by establishing new health insurance and hospital insurance plans. But today, it no longer wants this leadership. It is unfortunate that it will finally be the provinces who will be the victims of these drastic measures.
Of course, I agree with the minister that the situation has considerably improved in the field of health care, especially as concerns medical personnel. We have today a satisfying number of physicians, a good number of new graduates, but a number of them must now expatriate south of the border. We also have a surplus of nursing workers, human resources are there and the health resources fund has helped in various ways to develop that qualified personnel. However, all is not completed in the health care area.
An area which has been much forgotten is the one related to hospital administrators who have become needed because of the nature and complexity of the problems in health institutions. We must therefore develop efficient administrators for the smooth running of hospitals and to reduce some of the wastes occurring there. The work climate in certain hospitals is unbelievable or unbearable, which lead to the downgrading of health care. There are conflicts between medical and administrative personnel, lack of planning and in certain instances lack of discipline.
All that to say that the training of administrative personnel was neglected relative to the training of medical and nursing
personnel. The objectives of the health resources fund program must not be forgotten but redirected to meet new needs. At a time when the provinces must support an increase in part the whole financial burden of social and health services the federal government drops them without much consultation. I do not want to address those criticisms directly to the minister of course who, unfortunately, must abide by the decisions of cabinet on the spending cuts.
So there are areas for which we must do less and others for which we must do more. That is why I think those funds should not be cut but redirected to more urgent areas. One area I feel particularly strong about is that of preventive medicine, particularly in remote areas. Indeed, millions of dollars could be saved if we had personnel assigned to disease prevention. And how could one forget medical research.
In the very words of the minister in the debate last Thursday, over $100 million were assigned to research institutions through the health resources fund. Medical research is not only necessary but primordial in industrialized countries like ours. We know that federal contributions to research institutions have been cut somewhat for quite some time now. We even had examples of that in the area of fisheries and forestry.
Scientific research which requires considerable investments in technology and qualified personnel must nevertheless have all the necessary financial security so research projects will not be interrupted before they are completed. There can be no talk of restrictions when it comes to the health of people. No, Mr. Speaker, when it comes to the most precious asset of a people,
I do not think it should be a question of dollar signs. I am in favour of eliminating as much useless spending as possible but I will not be convinced that necessary programs should suffer unfairly from that epidemic of budget cuts. We must be careful. We might be criticized by future generations for having failed to make the necessary investments, to wit in essential areas such as those dealing with health care. We are gathered here to provide a better fate to all Canadians and we must not forget it. A well-known maxim says that health is priceless.
When I consider Bill C-2, it is not so much its contents which concern me but rather the fact that it is gathering weight and that we are told that other cuts will soon be made in the health area. Indeed it has already happened in the case of Indians. They did not appreciate the cuts suggested in their health scheme. They are therefore the most deprived in that connection. We only have to remember the mercury poisoning cases and still recently the high rate of tuberculosis cases which have been detected.
In conclusion Mr. Speaker, as I said earlier, I do not like cuts in the health field. I would rather have a more rational administration of health services so that each Canadian may be provided with every service available and enjoy his most precious asset, his health.

I see by tonight's press that the opposition is on both sides of that issue as well. The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) has said that they probably would not rule out a referendum if the case called for it. I think that the hon. member should read what his colleague has been saying before he makes comments like that.
With regard to the bill, I wanted to make a few comments because I once had the privilege of serving as parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. There have been a number of remarks made inside and outside this House by members opposite to the effect that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) and the Minister of Indian Affairs (Mr. Faulkner) were greatly cramping the health care extended to Indians. First of all, I thought it was unique that the opposition would debate this issue in association with this bill simply because this bill deals with the health resources fund, a program jointly shared by the federal government and the provinces in order to build health training facilities. It seems to be acceptable, however, in this debate to offer an opinion on almost any aspect of health care, no matter what it is, so I thought I would take this opportunity to respond to some of the comments which have been made about issues regarding native people.
If hon. members would review Hansard they would find questions and statements made to the Minister of National Health and Welfare which could give Canadians the idea that somehow the government was jeopardizing the lives of native people, that it was promoting suicide amongst them, and that it was causing undue hardship to them in terms of health care
Health Resources Fund Act
by depriving them of a basic service which all Canadians have a right to expect. I would like to clarify the record and indicate that the government, and I am sure this parliament as well, are not at all happy with the level of health among our native people and that we want it to be much better. This is certainly not the situation indicated by some of the members opposite.
In terms of infant mortality, in 1960 there were approximately 79 deaths per 1,000 live births. In 1976 the number decreased to 32.5 for native people. The comparative figures for the white population were 27 in 1960 and 14.3 in 1975 per 1,000. It is interesting to note that in the outlying and remote areas of Canada the rates are just about the same for both white people and native people. The death rate for Indians is almost the same, and their life expectancy is not much different. While there is room for improvement on these figures, I would like to indicate that the situation is certainly not as bad as members opposite have indicated.
I would like to comment on the guidelines the Minister of National Health and Welfare announced some time ago which have been the subject of questions and debate in the House and, indeed, were the prompting of a meeting between the minister, the National Indian Brotherhood and a number of Indian leaders. It was indicated by members opposite that somehow there had been a gearing down in health services offered to native people in Canada. That is not true. Surely members opposite know that primary health and hospital care are provided to the native people through the same medicare programs which are provided for non-native people across Canada.
In cases where there is hardship, as for example on reserves where there is no economic base, the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and, more specifically, the Department of National Health and Welfare, have spent a good of deal of money to increase their services and support to the program through hospitals, nursing stations, staffing of health care centres and through funds given directly to them.
The guidelines apply to the kinds of expenditures that are not covered, or what would be known as primary health care and hospital care situations, including eye glasses, dentures, prescription drugs and medical transportation services. I should like to put on the record the five things to which those guidelines referred: elective ground transportation by cars and taxis; elective dental care; supply of glasses, especially items such as special frames and tinting unless they were medically indicated; supply of non-prescription pharmaceuticals such as aspirins, tooth paste and hair shampoo. Individual Indians with incomes which are substantially greater than the provincial welfare limit are being asked to contribute to the cost of some of these items of health care as is the situation in the non-native community.
I think hon. members opposite should appreciate that it is incumbent upon the government to analyze these programs from time to time and, if there is waste, and if the administration is such that it is impossible to be sure the money is being well spent, then look at the guidelines. If the expenditure is not

necessary, surely that indicates the money will be subtracted from the basic health care. I am sure my colleagues would join me in arguing that discretionary health care expenditure should be as low as possible so that more money is available for the core activities that the native people need, deserve, and should have available to them. I think the debate in the House has revealed there are many situations that really do not relate to the basic health care but which are causing some problems in the native communities.
I do not share all the views of the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Smith), but I think he had a valid point today when he referred to some of the problems in regard to native housing. He used the example of an extremely cold house with a high humidity level, and pointed out that if it was sealed and insulated heavily to conserve heat, that may not be the most healthy situation. I would suggest, however, that many of the native problems are related to water supply and sewage, but these are not the kinds of things covered in Bill C-2. Hon. members opposite must know, if they have read the bill, that those are not the things that are indicated.
This afternoon the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) made a good speech and pointed out the advantages of a good lifestyle and how it could help improve health and thus decrease the cost of hospitalization and medical care. His point was well taken.
When the hon. member for Churchill spoke, he was very critical of the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) (Mrs. Campagnolo) for contributing to amateur sport. His argument was that the money should be going to health care. Surely if the minister's department is making contributions to a better lifestyle for a generation of Canadians, that will reduce their dependency on health care facilities. Is this not a better approach than funding programs that may or may not be essential for basic health care?
When the Minister of National Health and Welfare met with Indian leaders to discuss this subject, she told them that her department will be most willing to review any cases of individual hardship reported to it. I understand from her parliamentary secretary that to date no cases have been drawn to the department's attention.
The minister was careful to point out to the Indian community that an appeal procedure was contained in the guidelines which could be followed by anyone who felt they were unduly harsh. Also, in order to set aside any of the basic concerns in the native community, the minister agreed to delay implementation of the guidelines for a six-month period. This was conditional upon there being consultation at the band council level with local officials of her department and of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. The discussion would then advance to the regional level and, as it matured to the national level the National Indian Brotherhood would be involved and, I suspect also, the cabinet committee. This consultative process should be productive in this case as well as on other issues affecting the native people, the Department of National Health and Welfare and the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
The minister went further and agreed to fund the process. If any case of hardship is drawn to the attention of either department, hon. members opposite can be assured it will be dealt with. If the native people have genuine concerns, the consultative process has been established and is financed by the government.
Another point is the recognition that it is not either a treaty or aboriginal right to provide the kind of health care about which we have been talking. It is just the social policy of this government that has been supported by virtually every member of this and preceding parliaments that have wanted native people to have good health care and were prepared to make sure that the funding is available. In view of the debate that has taken place both inside and outside this House, Mr. Speaker, I just want to comment that this is not a new policy. It relates to the expenditure of money for ground transportation, cars, taxis, dental care that the individual likes to take on his own, the supply of glasses, tinted glasses, special frames, non-prescribed drugs, tooth paste, hair shampoo, aspirin, and also the requirement of asking individuals-be they native people-to pay if they can afford to, as is the case in the white communities.
I think both the Department of National Health and Welfare and the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development have done a commendable job of affording facilities to native people. Medical care and hospitalization are not affected, nor are essential or emergency services such as ambulance, air evacuation, supply of essential drugs or emergency dental care.
Not long ago I was in the far north, Mr. Speaker. The plane I was returning on was stopped and we were asked for eight volunteers to give up their seats so that a native person who had suffered a serious heart attack and another who required major surgery could be flown south to the best hospitals in Canada. It is a well established policy that natives in the outlying communities are flown to Yellowknife or Whitehorse, and if the medical attention and facilities there are not adequate they are then flown to Edmonton or Montreal, or wherever the facilities exist for them to have the same kind of medical attention that is available to any of us in this House.
The hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) inferred that the budget has been drastically cut and therefore is extremely unfair to the natives. That statement ignores the fact that the budget has been increased in this area. The total Indian health activity cost for salary and operating has been increased 13 per cent from the year 1977-78 to 1978-79. I wish to put on record the actual numbers. In 1977-78 it was increased from $78,188,000 to $88,677,000, an increase of some 13 per cent.
In the non-insured services to all Indians, in 1974-75 the department spent approximately $17.5 million. That was increased in the year 1975-76 to $2214 million, an increase of 27 per cent. In 1976-77 it was increased to $24million, a further 10 per cent increase. In the year 1977-78 it was

February 5, 1979

increased to $27.4 million, a further 12 per cent. In the budget year 1978-79 the total is $30 million, a further 10 per cent increase.
In terms of the government's commitment to adequate funding for medical care and facilities for native people, there can be no question that even with the over-all government policy of restraint this budget item has been substantially increased in the last five budget years, ranging anywhere from 10 per cent to 27 per cent.
I wish to speak to the hon. member's last point in connection with the guidelines. He stated that individual Indians with incomes substantially greater than the provincial welfare limit would be asked to defray some of the costs themselves. That is a standard situation across Canada. People well know that those items not covered in a province under the basic health care plan must be paid for by the individual. If they are in a situation where they are elderly, have a very limited income or a disability and are unable to earn income, there are provincial programs that will assist them. In the case of native people, there are federal assistance programs. In those areas where there is no economic base for the native people to earn income, assistance is available.
There are a number of native people who have very substantial incomes. In terms of trying to maximize the health care provided with the $30 million that has been budgeted, it seems only right that those who have the ability could and should pay. Most of the money should go to assist those who genuinely need it.
In conclusion, I again say that I appreciate the opportunity to enter this debate. I wanted to clarify for those who have been alarmed that somehow the government is cutting back on health care services to Canada's native people that the opposite is the case. In spite of restraint this year, the budget has been increased by 10 per cent. The guidelines only address themselves to discretionary spending in the health care area, asking that that be looked at a second time and to verify or authorize before expenditures are made. They ask that native people who can afford those items be asked to pay for them. I would be very surprised if many Indian leaders argued with that point. In adjusting its social programs, the government is trying to direct more money to where the need is greatest and perhaps not as much to where the need is not so evident. With those remarks, Mr. Speaker, I thank you for the opportunity to participate.
