speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have heard a great deal of debate on this bill which is very loosely related to the provisions of the bill itself. In fact we have heard from the government side a self-congratulating account of how it first came to invade the field of health care in the 1960s, forcing reluctant provinces into cost sharing programs on which it has since unilaterally welched. Speakers on the government side, of course, have taken the strange tack of praising themselves for the good work they did in setting up these health care programs, when in fact the whole substance of this bill has to do with knocking down the health resources program. Members on the government side might benefit from
Health Resources Fund Act
reading the bill again. It is only one paragraph long in its essential part. All it says is that the government is backing out of its commitment to the provinces two years early.
Three years ago I had occasion to join in debate on another bill in which the government was backing out of another aspect of its commitment to the provinces. In the mid-1960s the government held out a financial carrot to the provinces to force them into cost-sharing medicare programs. Provincial health ministers could see then that the carrot was rotten, but since the federal government had drawn to itself so much control over government spending and over programs that belong in provincial jurisdiction, the only alternative was to accept this rotten carrot or to be denied funds that were being offered to other provinces.
The result of joining these cost sharing programs was that the provinces became involved in increasingly costly programs whose costs have been escalating through the 1970s to dizzying heights. Ontario had already embarked upon a health care program that suited its own needs as a province. The Liberal government in Ottawa put it in a position of having to opt for the shared program put forward by the federal government, and it has been saddled with that program since.
I do not suggest for a moment that health costs have risen only because the federal government is involved in them. Costs have risen in almost any direction we care to look in the service industries. On the other hand, the pace at which costs escalate can be controlled in certain ways. If the provinces had been left free to find their own solutions to the escalation in health care costs, they might well have been saved from the problems they find themselves faced with when the federal government, finding the heat in the kitchen too much for it, decides to quit and suddenly abandons the programs into which it had forced the provinces.
Medicare costs are not the direct issue in this present bill, but they provide the means of getting at the principle underlying the bill. The government is doing the same thing it did three years ago when it decided unilaterally to throttle the cost-shared program commitment it had made with the provinces. At that time, finding that it was spending more than it wanted to be involved in spending, it simply sat down and said in effect, "We don't like the terms of the agreement any more; we're going to cut back on it." Now, once again, it is doing the same thing with a program it set up with the provinces.
Three years ago when the government decided to renege on its medicare commitments, I said, thinking of my own province of Ontario, "We knew at the outset that the provincial medical care program was superior to the federal program that we were asked to join. We also knew what we were dealing with in this case. There was no way we could be sure that the federal government would honour this agreement. We, like the other provinces, knew that this government's record of keeping its word was hardly conducive to placing very much faith in this particular federal-provincial agreement." Well, Mr. Speaker, sadly but predictably, I say the same thing again today about the program which is being thrown out in the present bill.

February 5, 1979
Health Resources Fund Act
The principle involved here, Mr. Speaker, is the principle of good faith. A government that bargains in good faith does not commit itself to particular levels of spending for particular periods of time and then, without consultation and agreement, announce a change of heart. In the previous bill three years ago, the government pleaded that health costs were rocketing out of control. It couldn't stand the heat. It wanted out. Well, this time the government cannot use that excuse, Mr. Speaker, because it sponsored the program which is being scuttled in this bill, a program to increase the health care training facilities in Canada and committed to it an amount of $500 million. Now, having decided that the way to save its own neck is to cut back on spending, it has found this program and has discovered that by chopping it, it can announce a saving of $84 million.
The costs of this program can certainly not be said to have rocketed out of control. The funds were voted for it back in the mid 1960s-$500 million to be spent over a 15-year period. As other speakers have pointed out, those dollars have shrunk mightily by today's standards. Accordingly, inflation has already taken a great toll on the program's funding. Now, two years before it had said the program would end, the federal government wants to end it, dealing yet another blow to the building up of health care facilities across Canada.
There are two ways of looking at the principle underlying the bill, Mr. Speaker. There is the way suggested by the minister when she introduced it. She told us the program had already been 83 per cent spent and had therefore accomplished many of its purposes. Accordingly, she regards it as an easy program from which to steal, to make up the budget cuts to which the government is committed. But there is another way of viewing the principle underlying the bill. It is that the government, seeing itself in disfavour with the electorate throughout the country and realizing that its wild spending habits over the past few years have landed the country in enormous trouble, is looking for a way to save its skin. It has sifted through its programs looking for ways to appear to save money without losing too many votes. Looked at in these terms, this bill has very little to do with good government and a lot to do with this government as it tries to save its own skin.
If the program was good in its conception, then the government should have the courage to maintain its level of funding, especially considering how much more cheaply the government comes by this amount of money these days. Even if it were a flawed program, unilateral decisions to cut off bilateral agreements are far from civilized. They are so close to the law of the jungle that no government which cares to keep good faith with its electorate would ever be guilty of them.
When the Trudeau government suddenly cut the funding of its shared-cost medical aid program three years ago, we in Ontario were faced with the threat of hospital closings in many communities. Now, once again in Ontario we are faced with the possibility that a new fee may be levied on chronic care patients who stay in hospital more than 60 days. There are no easy solutions to the problems of cost in such social programs

as these, Mr. Speaker. For that reason, governments must work all the harder to make sure their programs are intelligently conceived and responsibly carried out. How can the provinces plan long-term programs if they are bound to the federal government in a shotgun marriage which always threatens a sudden divorce? How can Ontario-to refer again to my own province-maintain the level of health care it had planned for its citizens if the federal government keeps twisting in the wind? Why did the Liberal government railroad the provinces into these shared-cost programs at all if it has the gall later to leave them hanging?
One fact is obvious. When the federal government leaves a provincial government in the lurch these days, it is never a Liberal government which is affected. The voters have seen to that. And perhaps that is why the Trudeau government has the gall to practice cost-cutting in this way. It forces the provincial governments to cut back on services and the provincial governments, except for the one in Prince Edward Island which will probably not be there long, are not Liberal. Perhaps the Trudeau government hopes, in this way, to stir the anger of the electorate against other parties. But people have lived with this government long enough not to be fooled.
When a user fee becomes necessary for long-term hospital patients in Ontario, the voters of that province will know that it is a Trudeau fee they are being asked to pay. It is a fee for having a Prime Minister in Ottawa who reneges on commitments. In provinces like Ontario the voters are already anxiously waiting for the Trudeau government to get out of the kitchen. The government cannot keep its promises, and the deceptiveness coming out of the goverment kitchen is no longer acceptable to the people.
In terms of the Ministry of National Health and Welfare specifically, the country is already aware of the many aspects of bad administration that prevent programs from operating smoothly and efficiently. Last night we saw a confused health minister appearing on television after the late news to explain the unexplainable to us in terms of the child tax credit. Mothers who have never been asked to fill out income tax forms before are now required to jump through a bureaucratic hoop that even the minister didn't seem to understand. Similarly, many will also have to apply for a social insurance number. And senior citizens who are accustomed to filing their tax forms early in the hope of receiving an early tax rebate must suffer the very considerable inconvenience of waiting in line to get their T-4 slips at the end of February, whilst the minister of health tries to work her way through the jungle of her own red tape.
If the provinces had been given warning that the government was reneging on its commitment, Mr. Speaker, we might have been able to take comfort from the fact that at least the minister of health was giving up trying to run one program. Shortly we shall be able to take comfort from the fact that she won't be running anything. In the meantime, we are faced with the bill before us, which leaves the provinces in the lurch and gives the government an opportunity to say it has saved money.
February 5, 1979

As other speakers have pointed out, every dollar spent improving medical research and extending health training, especially in preventive medicine, saves many dollars in later health care costs. If we are to have truly effective health care, then some of the money which the federal government is saving will no doubt have to be spent by the provinces. What we are faced with in this bill is one more piece of face-saving legislation by a worn-out government.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to speak on this bill, primarily because of what it reveals about the way in which the government is dealing with its own understanding of restraint. The minister has indicated that the program we have had since 1966 has been a good program. I think all members of this House have agreed that it has been good and useful in a number of ways. According to her own words, the minister has reluctantly come to the conclusion that because of the need for restraint it is necessary to cut the remaining funds under the program, 83 per cent having been spent. It seems to me that there are three or four things that this reveals about the way the government is going about its business in this matter.
First let me deal with the question of research and development. I think it was June 1 of last year when the government indicated that it wished to re-establish its credentials and become enthusiastic about a policy for stimulating research and development, particularly in the fields of science and technological growth. That was the way the government wished to proceed from then on in. What we see with this bill today is another example of the difference between words and reality. I would like to cite a few statistics with respect to the government's commitment to research and development, and many more could be gathered.
The government has cut out S8.5 million from the support of science in the Department of Agriculture. The government has cut funding of $3 million from the extension to the Lethbridge research laboratory, $2.8 million in contributions toward construction of veterinary colleges, $2.7 million from the Canadian Dairy Commission for product research and promotion programs, $.8 million in grants to universities for water resources research, $1.4 million from the Alberta Oil Sands environment research program, $700,000 from stratospheric research, $2.7 million from the pollution abatement technology program, $2.8 million from the Newfoundland environment centre and maritime forest research centre and $11.1 million from the Department of Fisheries.
There are many examples outside the field of medical research where, over the years, we have seen a continuing cutting away from research and development funds, particularly in the fields of science and technological growth.
It is worth while pointing out that the Medical Research Council is responsible for approximately half of all the biomedical research funding in Canada. Let us look at the record in terms of the government's commitment to research and development in that field. In terms of the total budget of
Health Resources Fund Act
the Department of National Health and Welfare, the Medical Research Council's budget has fallen from 1.33 per cent in 1971 to 1.3 per cent in 1972, to 1.14 per cent in 1973, to .87 per cent in 1974, and currently it is batting about .6 per cent. I think that should be underlined because it is a reduction, in the short space of seven years, by two thirds in the field of medical research as it pertains to the ability of the Medical Research Council to obtain funds from the minister's department. That is not a policy of stimulating research and development. That is a policy of constantly cutting back, and it is very much a false economy.
There are a number of reasons why research and development, particularly in the medical field, are important, not the least of which is to remember that the end product of research is prevention. Research is designed to prevent the occurrence of disease and ill health. It seems to me that it is significant that where we might understand restraint in all other forms of industry, enterprise or business, the government fails to understand it when it comes to medical research. The importance of long-term research is that it diminishes the cost of health care. Therefore, to cut off funds at the research and development stage is indeed a false economy. However, it is not something which does not affect people. It affects people very directly because it affects them with regard to something which ultimately matters to them most, that is, their health.
It appears to me, particularly in the last ten years, that when it comes to the crunch and when it comes to cutting out funds, we always make sure that we cut off our future. This government is saying that in the name of restraint it is going to have to cut medical research, which will have the effect of establishing new procedures and new technology with respect to preventing ill health and with respect to providing health care for those who suffer from ill health.
Perhaps it is even more significant, but in an entirely different direction, that when we cut off research programs, particularly in fields which are scientifically sophisticated, we lose not only what we might have gained from research, but we also lose researchers. This country has seen generation after generation of people having to go either to the south, over to Europe, or somewhere else, because the sorry history of this country, especially under this government, has been not to put dollars into improving our future, particularly as that relates to health care.
That is something which is difficult to measure because we cannot measure how many good medical researchers and how many good medical teams are broken up when funds are cut off. This does not mean that we will not finally have the technology. It does not mean that we will not finally enjoy the fruits of that research. We will, as we always have, import it from other countries which are getting information and knowledge from Canadians who have left Canada because they have to go elsewhere to find facilities with which to do their research. That, in miniature, is the way this government deals with the question of research and development. Despite protestations about wanting to stimulate research and development,

February 5, 1979
Health Resources Fund Act
both inside and outside medical research the government has followed a policy of diminishing them.
The second thing which is revealed about the government is its total insensitivity to the significance of making sure that important programs which affect provinces are undertaken after consultation. This is a matter which many hon. members have raised. It has been raised with regard to almost every program the government has decided either to stop or start. It takes no great intelligence to remember that other governments-not just the federal government-require predictability. Indeed, those who are served and affected by programs also need predictability. That is particularly so in the field of research. We cannot just start and stop research programs. This is even more important in the medical field.
When this matter was before the House at second reading, I understand that some minister indicated that there was no contract or agreement signed and sealed with the provinces. However, whether there was a signed and sealed contract which would be enforceable in a court of law is not the point. Surely when a province made an agreement with the federal government 13 years ago, it expected the program would last the length of time it was supposed to last and, indeed, it might perhaps have been in the interests of medical research, the provinces and the people, if the program were to last longer. It is not a question of legally enforceable contracts; it is a question of trust. Again this government finds itself not worrying or caring whether programs will adversely affect the provinces or, indeed, the people.
There is a third aspect which I think should have been brought to the attention of the minister. Much research in this country is done by voluntary organizations. If the government was going to cut the program two years before the end of its natural life, it might at least have tried to find out if certain voluntary organizations could take over some aspects of the program, given the existing funding commitments, in order that the program would not be affected or cut sharply. The federal government has not been able to come to grips with coping with voluntary organizations as it goes through its program of restraint. [DOT]
Merely because the government decides not to carry out a program does not mean the need dies. When those government services are withdrawn, surely it is incumbent upon the government to see whether there are voluntary organizations to take up the slack. Indeed it is possible that there will be some funding, but not nearly as much as the government had pledged under this particular program. I might emphasize perhaps that is more important in the field of geriatric services. The government is on record, in a speech by the minister, on caring about the needs of the aged in our society. I believe the minister referred to a new deal for the aged. At least she is sincere in her view. The fact of the matter is that there has been absolutely no attempt by the government to find ways for voluntary organizations to assist Canadians, as it

withdraws funds and cuts services and programs which affect a great many people.
Also it is worthy of note that the government has seen fit to withdraw funds from programs which will affect both directly and ultimately those people who are least able to cope for themselves. Everyone who has any experience at all at the receiving end knows that when teaching and training facilities are cut, particularly in the health care field, the services most affected are those to people who are old, poor and handicapped. Those are the funds which go first.
I do not think there is a member on the government side who would step forward and say, "We would like to reduce training services for people being trained to help handicapped people." Government members will not say that. They do not wish to say that, but that is what they are doing. In the final analysis the poor, old and handicapped are not defeated by a direct assault. It is an entire series of subtle withdrawals of programs which were in place to help them out. These programs are slowly eroded away by what used to be called the old trickle down theory. By and large what happens is that the people who would ordinarily be taking courses and learning skills, particularly in health care training, will not be given the necessary funds. Therefore the services which will go are those such as home care, meals on wheels, and others. Slowly they are worn away, they are eroded. Thus, the ultimate effect of this cut will be borne by those who can least afford it.
I was pleased to participate in the discussion of the bill before the House for the following reasons: first, although 83 per cent of the program has been delivered, as it were, and although the minister can argue that by and large the objectives have been reached, anybody who wants to listen will realize that, despite what the government says, it does not stand for stimulating research and development programs. Its record is entirely in the opposite direction. Second, it continues to create divisions in the country by not dealing in an appropriate manner with the mechanism of consultation with the provinces. Third, it seems to have lost its understanding of the significance and importance of voluntary organizations which would be happy to be in this business if the government withdrew. Fourth, it is easier to withdraw funding for programs which affect those people who cannot speak loud enough to be heard. For those reasons, the bill does not deserve the support of the House.

Yes, Mr. Speaker. Yet is it not passing strange that the minister, who challenged each of us to get a commitment from our provinces that the amount of the child tax credit would not be deducted from welfare payments, could not get that same commitment from her own province of Quebec, notwithstanding the unusual relationship she must enjoy with the government of Quebec because she represents the Government of Canada, she is a minister holding a senior portfolio within the Government of Canada?
Again we see the consequences of the failure of this government to consult adequately with the provinces, because if there had been adequate consultation, if the Minister of National Health and Welfare had called together the various social services ministers of the ten provinces and sat down with them and took them into her confidence, and told them the government would bring in an amendment to the Family Allowances Act and would make provisions for a child tax credit of $200 per child but it wanted an assurance from each one of the provinces that they would not deduct the amount of this child tax credit allowance from the welfare payments that they presently have in place, I believe that provincial governments are reasonable and, when confronted with that kind of reasonable proposition, would respond positively. I am sure that the minister would have been able to obtain an undertaking that no such deduction would be made from the amount of welfare paid.
I talk about the amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act in which, again because of lack of consultation, we had the unique, the practically unprecedented situation of the ten provinces of this country saying, "We are just not going to take it any more". They came together and they appeared before the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration and bemoaned the fact that there had been no consultation, notwithstanding the impact that the changes in unemployment insurance would have on the provincial economies, especially on the eastern provinces, and they put forward

positive proposals of their own, proposals which they should have been given the opportunity of making at a federal-provincial meeting.
God knows, we have had enough federal-provincial conferences. Indeed, one wonders about the relevancy of this place when one considers what is going on across the street at the old converted Union station. That has become the real parliament in this city. That is where the action is, and that perhaps explains why the Minister of National Health and Welfare is not in her place tonight. Perhaps she knows that the real decisions are to be made across the street.
If this place is to be relevant and meaningful in terms of its legislative capacity, then I say we have to dig in when the government confronts parliament with a bill of this kind that represents a major breach of faith with the provinces of this country. If we have to dig in, let us dig in, and what better way to dig in?
It is all very well for the minister to talk about the fact that 83 per cent of the program has been completed. Do we ever arrive at the stage where we have completed medical research in this country? Medical research will never end. Indeed, by its very nature it can never end. I believe when this statute was passed by this House 13 years ago the government of the day never had the intention of repealing it. I believe there was an implicit understanding, when the bill was passed, that when the 15-year period was up there would be another program to replace and, indeed, to enlarge upon it.
The fact of the matter is that we are abrogating a solemn undertaking made to the provinces 13 years ago. Why is that so? I suggest it is to save $83 million. The government of this day is embarking upon a spending program that hovers between $45 billion and $50 billion, yet we are taking about $83 million to complete an undertaking to the provinces to provide funding for medical research in this country.
What about the programs that will have to be cancelled, and the research teams which have been brought together and will be lost to this country as a result of the cancellation of this program? I can speak from experience in my own province, that province rich in promise yet so poor in its ability to deliver. We have the newest medical school in the country at the Memorial University of Newfoundland. It is a credit to this country. I would suggest that a large part of the ongoing biomedical research at the Memorial University was made possible by this health resources fund program. The people at that medical school tell me this new institution is going to lose this medical expertise which has been gathered together. That medical school will lose this expertise because it does not have the funding to carry on biomedical research, research in geriatric and family medical practice, those things relatively unsophisticated, yet important things that other medical schools in the country no longer carry out.
What do I say to these people at the university? Where are they to go? Where are they going to look for funding? How can the people involved in a professional research capacity
February 5, 1979

have any confidence in the Government of Canada to fulfil its promise? The answer, of course, is that we will lose these people, as has been so eloquently stated by my friend from Toronto, the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie), and as has been demonstrated by my learned colleague, the hon. member for Athabasca. We will lose these people to the United States, which is perhaps the intention of this government which seems to be able to come up with dollars from some kind of hidden fund to provide sexy political programs in order to fund arenas in large cities in this country for the National Hockey League, an area in which we have a questioned right to be involved.
Perhaps we will lose these people for ever. What will happen then? I suppose then we will go back to the point we were at 13, 14, 15 years ago when most of the medical research done in this country was funded by endowments from the United States. Is that where we want to be, and is that the kind of situation we want in this country? I submit there is not a Canadian who, given the facts, would support that proposition. That is why I believe this bill, innocent though it may appear, and presented in a manner that would indicate it is a mere housekeeping bill, is a blot on the already tarnished image of this government.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
I could ask where the $18 million is to be derived. Is it to come from the $83 million to be saved by cancelling this program? Is that the source of these funds? We have a right to an answer to that question. Is that where the $18 million is coming from in order to improve the image of the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) and perhaps to gain a few political yards in those big cities across the country? Perhaps this money is to come from the government's Outreach Program which was cancelled or restricted last year to exclude women. We know about that retrograde step which set back progress in this country by 25 years when it was announced that women would no longer be targets of the Outreach Program. How much was saved by that discriminatory act? Did it save $18 million, enough to finance these arena improvements in Winnipeg, Edmonton, and Quebec City? Where did the money come from? We have a right to know. Did it come partially from the $2 million the government is to save in terms of cutting back on the publications it now makes available for university libraries in this country?
I had to tell the people at my university library that if the government cancels this program they should let me know and I will make the publications available to them if I have access to them. What kind of a misguided sense of priorities is possessed by this government? Why would it eliminate a $2 million program to provide technical publications to the university libraries in this country? What kind of restraint is that? What kind of misguided restraint is it? This is not restraint; this is a facade, a joke, and a misrepresentation of the word "restraint". Nobody expects that kind of restraint.
Nobody expects the Government of Canada to cut back on its commitment to universities, just as nobody in this country
Health Resources Fund Act
would expect the Government of Canada to cut back on its solemn obligation made to the provinces of this country 13 years ago to provide an ongoing program of research in the universities and medical research institutes.
An. hon. Member: It is counter productive.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
The hon. member suggests this move is counter productive and that it will cost us dearly in the years ahead.
I hope somebody else will take the floor before this bill is allowed to receive third reading. I hope the hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray), for whom I have great respect, will get to his feet and express his concern over what the government is doing. Perhaps we may even hear from other hon. members. Surely this House of Commons, if it has any sense of responsibility, has the ongoing, solemn responsibility to ensure that commitments outlined by statute to the provinces of this country are honoured and not abrogated by repeal as is happening in the case of this bill now before the House.
I suspect, indeed I know that all is not well within the Department of National Health and Welfare.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: That is what the newspapers say.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
That is what the newspapers say, and I suspect they know what they are talking about. I believe that if we were able to examine the qualified, capable and dedicated men and women who advise the Minister of National Health and Welfare we would find that they agree with us, and that this act should not be repealed. I suspect that they would also agree with our contention that there must be an ongoing consultation, given the limited jurisdiction of the Government of Canada, in some of these areas, particularly the areas of social policy. The fact that the newspapers have identified that there are problems would indicate to me that they have put their finger on the nub of the situation.
I could go on, Mr. Speaker, and talk about nutrition, child health care, geriatrics, pediatrics and obstetrics, all of which require ongoing research in this country. I could go on and talk about the International Year of the Child and the need for ongoing studies with regard to nutrition, dental care, day care, and immunization. The findings of the nutritional survey of a few years ago, funded by the people of Canada at great expense, for example, identified what is nothing short of a national scandal in this country, the fact that we have a serious problem of malnutrition. It is hard to believe that there is malnutrition and diet deficiency in our young people in this affluent society. It said that our children at age 12 had a physical capability comparable to a 30-year-old Swede. This is all due to inadequate diet, junk food in our schools, and television, as my hon. friend identified, which teaches these children to eat this junk food but does not identify the fact that it has little or no nutritional value.
I could go on and talk about the seriousness of the problem of native people. Indeed, that was a question which came up

February 5, 1979
Health Resources Fund Act
during the course of the debate on the child tax credit bill when we implored that the government make the child tax credit allowance available in quarterly payments because many of the mothers who would be receiving the one large lump sum do not have the experience of managing that amount of money and, as a result, the money would not find its way to the purposes for which parliament intended.
Canada does not have a school lunch program. There is a school lunch program in the United States, and there has been so for many years. There is no suggestion in Canada, however, of sitting down with the provinces and saying, "Look, we have a major problem in this country, our children are undernourished, and because of that undernourishment their learning process is retarded." Our children are more regressive because they are going to school without an adequate breakfast, because there is an iron deficiency in their diet, because they are drinking too much soda pop, because they are taking too much junk cereal, and because they are drinking too much.
Alcoholism among our children has become a major problem, more serious than the soft drug problem. Our kids are getting high on beer and are drinking beer and alcohol on an empty stomach, yet we see the Government of Canada abdicating its responsibility. Why can there not be a program of alcohol education for our young children? Why can they not be told that alcohol, if taken in moderation, is something to be enjoyed, but if abused it can lead to addiction or danger to one's health? In spite of this we tolerate advertising in this country which presents alcohol drinking as a lifestyle to be desired, ads which are sophisticated and almost subliminal in their techniques in trying to hook our kids on X or Y or Z brands of beer, knowing full well that once they have them, they have them for life. But nothing is done in the area of alcohol education on a national basis.
Perhaps nothing is done because of the power of the advertising industry. I do not know. I understand that the breweries of this country spend approximately $30 million on advertising. That is a hell of a big advertising budget by any stretch of the imagination. Perhaps some of these advertising agencies which handle these accounts are friends of the government and that is why it is a no-no.
We did not hear from the Minister of National Health and Welfare, who likes to talk about social policy as though she had the market cornered, on this matter. This government is bankrupt when it comes to social policy, because it has no social policy. If there was a social policy it would not bring in this kind of bill at this particular time. If there was a social policy, there would be an ongoing education program in an attempt to offset some of the dangerous nutritional habits of our young people, a program to provide for adequate day care for single parent families, and to provide adequate day care for family situations where both parents must work in order to offset the consequences of inflation. There would also be programs for instructing young people who assume family responsibilities, as they are doing at a younger and younger age in this country.
This bill would have provided the Minister of National Health and Welfare with an opportunity to come before this House and tell us her concerns about where this country is going. She has not done so, because I do not think she has any concern. I do not think that she really cares. I regret to have to say that in her absence. I would prefer to say that to her face, but she is not here.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: The parliamentary secretary is here.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
The parliamentary secretary is here; albeit he arrived a little late, but he is here. The Minister of State (Multiculturalism), the Minister of Labour, and all kinds of ministers are here, but we do not have the minister responsible for this bill, yet she would like us to give it third reading although it violates a solemn obligation made to the provinces to provide ongoing medical research. To what end? To save $83 million, when in the same breath we can save $18 million allocated to fund NHL stadiums in Winnipeg, Edmonton, Hamilton, and Quebec city for professional sports.
We have facilities in my city of St. John's which we put together for the Summer Games. We are proud of what we did in the Summer Games, but those facilities were closed down for a year because we did not have the money to operate them. We could not get any help from the federal governent to operate our beautiful aqua-arena or any of the marvellous facilities we put together to host the young athletes of this country in the Canada Games. Yet we can find $18 million for the National Hockey League in those big cities. What a misguided sense of priority; what a government!
I see, Mr. Speaker, that you are getting ready to rise. May I call it ten o'clock?

subtopic: FOREIGN INVESTMENT REVIEW ACT-INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH PRINCIPLES OF INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS CONDUCT
FOREIGN INVESTMENT REVIEW ACT-INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH PRINCIPLES OF INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS CONDUCT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on July 18, 1975, the then minister of industry, trade and commerce tabled in this House on behalf of the government what he called the "new principles of international business conduct." At that time he said they were "intended as an updating and replacement of the guiding principles of good corporate behaviour in Canada." These had been announced by the late hon. Robert Winters on March 31, 1966, when he was minister of industry, trade and commerce. When the minister of industry, trade and commerce who is now the Minister of

February 5, 1979

Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) tabled the new set of principles he said they reflected "broad government policy regarding the activities and responsibilities of foreign controlled business enterprises in Canada." He made it clear, as he said, that "they are directed toward all foreign controlled enterprises whether they were involved with the Foreign Investment Review Act or not."
According to a press report early last week, however, officials of several foreign controlled firms in Canada do not seem to be aware of these important principles. The author of the article in question could not find any indication that the government was really monitoring the degree of compliance by such companies with these principles. Yet, when they were tabled in this House in 1975, they were described by the then minister of industry, trade and commerce as "broad government policy".
I gather from what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said in this House last week that this policy is still in force. If this is the case, then the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce must have in place, or must set up as soon as possible, a program to bring forcefully to the attention of senior management of all foreign controlled companies in Canada these new and important principles of international business conduct.
It is not surprising that the companies which were contacted by the journalist about the matter told him they had not heard of these principles. After all, senior executives change fairly frequently; they transfer, retire, assume new responsibilities. Therefore there must be an ongoing effort by the government to remind directly all foreign controlled businesses of these principles. Interestingly enough, that was the approach used by Mr. Winters when he announced the first version of these principles. He also had his department set up a survey to monitor the degree of compliance by foreign controlled companies with these principles. The survey was carried out by regularly sending out questionnaires to a representative sample of foreign controlled companies. The results were published for some years. However, the last publication of the results of the survey was in 1974, to cover only the years 1971 and 1972. The parliamentary library has no later publication of the results of this survey in its collection.
The purpose of the survey is important. It is to assess the degree of voluntary compliance with these principles which in effect call for the application of the FIRA test of "significant benefit" by all foreign controlled companies, including those not covered by that law. Therefore, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) at the very least should publish information updating these survey results. He should reinstitute this survey if, in fact, it was dropped some years ago as appears to be the case. At the very least as well, as I have said, he should ensure the principles of international business conduct are brought regularly to the attention of senior executives of all foreign controlled companies in Canada.
But if these principles were and are government policy, meaning something the government believes should be carried out in the public interest, then the government must soon take steps to ensure there is compliance in fact with that govern-
Adjournment Debate
ment policy it calls the "new principles of international business conduct." It should do this to help accomplish the necessary aim of further expanding employment and economic activity generally in Canada.
The high level of foreign control of our economy is emerging again as a significant political issue in Canada. This is confirmed by a recent Gallup poll showing a high degree of public concern about this high level of control. I believe the government must respond to this concern in a meaningful way if it is to be re-elected by the Canadian people in the coming election. A pledge of action by the government, not just to recognize the benefits but also to deal with the costs to the Canadian economy of this high level of foreign control of our economy, is needed now and in the coming weeks to ensure the re-election of the government but, more important, to assure the long term best interests of the Canadian people.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bernard Loiselle (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: FOREIGN INVESTMENT REVIEW ACT-INQUIRY AS TO COMPLIANCE WITH PRINCIPLES OF INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS CONDUCT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, following their approval in 1975 the new guidelines were distributed to all companies through the information kit provided by FIRA. Those guidelines were also published in the businessman's guide by FIRA and in the FIRA review for 1977. The guide is distributed to companies dealing with FIRA. The review was sent to most financial branches operating in Canada. As for the other question, that is when the results of our survey will be made available and published, it is advisable to point out that the guidelines cannot be effectively controlled on a statistical basis alone. My department is carrying out a voluntary survey among the main branches of foreign companies. The hon. member was right when he said that the results of the last survey were published in 1974. However, the results of the survey up to 1975 were published in May 1978. The data covering the activities for the period ending in 1977 will probably be published in April, 1979. We hope that those results will be effectively used to consider some aspects of operations in foreign-controlled branches. The passage of the amendment in Bill C-3 concerning the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act will surely provide a more effective control and assessment of operations in foreign-controlled branches.
And allow me to say, Mr. Speaker, that in spite of all written instructions which could be tabled today in the House the best guarantee which can be provided is still the daily control made by officials who are anxious to ensure the sound operation of Foreign Investment Review Agency.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to continue the line of questioning pursued by the hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray), a former cabinet

February 5, 1979
Adjournment Debate
minister. I am sure the same parliamentary secretary will read two or three answers tonight.
I rose in my place on October 23 to inquire of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) regarding the purchase of Northwood Mills in Princeton, British Columbia, by Weyerhaeuser of the United States. I was following hard on questions posed by the hon. member for Okanagan-Kootenay (Mr. Johnston), as well as the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) who was not asking questions specifically about that but about the high percentage of approvals that FIRA gives to foreign takeovers of companies in Canada.
I would like to survey the situation at the moment. North-wood Mills is a Canadian company that is owned by Noranda, a wholly owned Canadian company. An American multinational wants to purchase it. I do not have anything against Weyerhaeuser. Generally speaking, it is a good corporate citizen.
Northwood does not want to sell to Weyerhaeuser. There is a group of small independent sawmills in the area. They realize their future is threatened if a large multinational comes into the vicinity. The wood industry is precarious. Frequently the margin of profit of these small independent sawmills depends on the sale of their chips.
If Weyerhaeuser purchases Northwood Mills and has an assured supply of chips for its pulp mill in Kamloops, it can do without these small independent sawmills. Naturally, these sawmills are a bit paranoid about this. They have formed a consortium to buy Northwood Mills rather than have it purchased by an American multinational.
FIRA in its true form of approving 85 to 90 per cent of all applications, has approved this application, when at the same time the Canadian small independents are wanting to improve their future. It is passing strange that the hon. member for New Westminster should have questioned the extent to which FIRA gives approval to multinationals while in this transaction the union, IWA, as well as the British Columbia president, Mr. Monroe, approved of the purchase by an American multinational of a Canadian company. The hon. member for New Westminster very sincerely asked about these approvals, yet here it is the unions which will support him in the next election which are saying "We would like to see this American multinational take over a wholly owned Canadian company."
I asked one of the directors about this. He said, "Well, the industry has to be integrated." Okay, the industry needs to be integrated, but must it be under the umbrella of one corporation? Surely, there could be co-operation among the small independents to keep the industry going-they have enough ingenuity for that. I cannot believe that it is the giant corporations which have built the strength into our economy which we have known historically. It is not the multinationals which have done it; it has been the risk taking and the initiative of the small independents.
We have now reached the point at which Weyerhaeuser effectively controls most of the Thompson River watershed

timber supply. One of the problems is that the company has overcut its supply of timber in the Lumby region of British Columbia and now wants the timber reserves owned by this mill in Princeton. We are now in a situation in which Canadian lumber dealers have to phone to an American company in the United States to place orders for Canadian lumber for resale. The first question Weyerhaeuser asks is, "Is there a Weyerhaeuser agent in that area?" And the company will not sell Canadian lumber to a Canadian agent if the lumber is going to a place where there is a Weyerhaeuser agent.
The minister tells me in the House that FIRA is so structured that it will not approve applications unless it is to the benefit of Canada. Yet here they are rubbing out jobs all over the place and we are allowing an American multinational to determine who can sell lumber and where it shall be sold. Is that for the advantage of Canadians? The fact is, the government believes in corporatism. Unions, too, believe in corporatism because they would much prefer to deal with a large corporation than with a number of independents. The package is a lot neater. This is especially true when very small sawmills are in the picture-operations which might not employ union workers.
Moreover, as we know, the corporations have only one certain way of handling competition and that is not through greater efficiency, it is by buying the competition out. So we face the grim prospect in this area of having one or two large companies controlling practically all of the lumber industry in the heart of British Columbia. I do not think the minister, through FIRA, has been acting in the best interests of Canada.
I have here a list of companies which were opting for the purchase of that mill. I notice Riverside Forest Products of Lumby, B.C., Gorman Brothers of Westbank; Aspen Planers of Merritt; Evans Forest Products of Savona; Wonnok Lumber of Mission; Gilbert Smith Forest Products of Barriere, and Drew Sawmill Limited of Malakwa, B.C., all of which said, "This ought to stay a Canadian concern; we object to an American multinational coming into the country and we want to preserve the integrity-"
Order. The time allotted to the hon. member has expired.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bernard Loiselle (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this presentation deals with two controversial points relating to the takeover of Northwood Mills Ltd. of Penticton by Weyerhaeuser Inc. of Tacoma, Washington. First, lumber retailers from the southern mainland of British Columbia might be forced to go to the United States to buy Canadian lumber from Weyerhaeuser. Second, it is feared that small independent sawmills will be separated from the markets buying their chips.
It is true that Canadian and American lumber retailers ordering Canadian lumber from Weyerhaeuser must dial the
February 5, 1979

toll-free telephone number Zenith 98676 which puts them in contact with that company's business section in Tacoma. The billing is made in that municipality. Remittances are sent to P.O. Box 4844 in Vancouver in Canadian funds and any correspondence with Weyerhaeuser must be addressed to 200 Consumer Road, Willowdale, Ontario. Of course, it is also true that practically all the lumber of that company is exported to the United States. It should be noted that even if the wholesale purchases are to be made in the United States Weyerhaeuser operates a number of retail outlets in Kamloops and elsewhere to serve British Columbia consumers.
Indeed, that company is not the only foreign-controlled corporation to centralize its operations in the United States but sometimes you have the opposite: a few foreign-owned corporations operating in Canada have opened in Canadian cities business outlets to serve Canadian and American retailers. Weyerhaeuser is thinking about establishing an outlet near Kamloops but one could consider that an attempt probably on the part of that good hon. member to compete more fiercely with local producers which could also trigger a reaction. As to the effects of this transaction on the small independent sawmills' ability to sell their chips, a comparison between the current situation and what is proposed will show that the effects will be quite negligible.
Just now, the Weyerhaeuser pulp mill in Kamloops is using
550.000	BD (Bone Dry) units of chips a year. Of these,
100.000	units are being provided by the Weyerhaeuser mills of
Adjournment Debate
the area, the rest being supplied by 21 independent sawmills. Weyerhaeuser can produce 190,000 units of chips in its own sawmills, but the current contracts with independent sawmills compel this corporation to reduce its deliveries of chips from its own sawmills in proportion with those of its independent suppliers. The sawmills in Northwood are producing 120,000 units of chips a year, but all their production is sold under contract to B.C. Forest Products Limited.
The independent sawmills are afraid that, as soon as their contracts with the B.C. Forest Products Limited expire, the chips produced by Northwood may be sold to the Weyerhaeuser sawmill, which would reduce the quantities this establishment would buy from them. Several factors are involved here. First of all, in case the contract between the Northwood and the B.C. Forest Products Limited is not renewed, it is to be expected that the latter will try to fill the gap by purchasing the same quantity of chips from the independent sawmills of the region.
